result.output:
1	# GraphMark
2	
3	A **reproducible, compiler-grounded** benchmark for code-intelligence "brains"
4	(tools that index a repository into a symbol + relation knowledge graph for AI
5	coding agents). It measures how accurately a brain recovers the **true** symbol
6	inventory and **true** static call graph of a codebase, scored against a
7	**tool-independent oracle** (the compiler), not against any tool's own output.
8	
9	> **Three suites live here.** This README documents the **Fidelity** benchmark
10	> (compiler oracle, graph correctness; Go + TypeScript) described below. The `competitive-eval/`
11	> directory is the **Tasks** suite — the multi-language, fixed-answer +
12	> agentic head-to-head migrated from `entire-plan` (see
13	> `competitive-eval/results/scoreboard.md`). The `agentic-swebench/` directory is the
14	> **Agentic-value** suite — does giving a coding agent the graph change how often (and how
15	> cheaply) it resolves real SWE-bench Multilingual issues, graded by the official swebench test
16	> harness (see `agentic-swebench/README.md`). The three measure different things
17	> (graph fidelity vs. retrieval usefulness vs. end-to-end agent value) and are reported
18	> separately; a fuller write-up of the multi-matrix model is planned.
19	
20	## Why this design
21	
22	Most code-intelligence benchmarks (including the tools' own) count *their own*
23	emitted symbols/relations — a number you inflate by emitting more. That measures
24	nothing. GraphMark instead uses the **Go compiler (`go/types`)** as ground
25	truth: the real set of declared functions/methods and the real call graph,
26	resolved through full type information. The compiler is the rubric, so the
27	comparison is fair across tools and reproducible by anyone.
28	
29	- **Identity is `(file, line)`** of a declaration. Every tree-sitter tool and the
30	  compiler agree on it because they parse the same bytes — no schema/ID
31	  normalization disputes.
32	- **Scope is intra-module** (callees resolved to a declaration inside the loaded
33	  packages) — exactly what a local repo brain can know.
34	- **`_test.go` is excluded symmetrically** from every side. (The oracle never
35	  parses test files; a brain that does would otherwise be unfairly penalized.
36	  This was a real fairness bug found while building the harness.)
37	
38	## Systems
39	
40	| system | what it is |
41	|---|---|
42	| `entire-sem` | the tree-sitter brain under test (`entire sem snapshot`) |
43	| `cbm` | **DeusData/codebase-memory-mcp** — tree-sitter + Hybrid LSP; the head-to-head competitor (`codebase-memory-mcp cli ...`), run at full strength (Hybrid LSP active for Go) |
44	| `naive` | name-match floor: link a call to **every** in-module function sharing the callee's name, with no type resolution. Shows what real resolution buys. |
45	| *oracle* | `go/types` ground truth (the ceiling, not a competitor) |
46	
47	## Reproduce
48	
49	```sh
50	# 1. Build the oracle (compiler ground truth) and the entire-sem binary.
51	go build -o /tmp/graphmark-bin/oracle ./cmd/oracle
52	go build -o /tmp/graphmark-bin/entire-sem <path-to-entire-sem>/cmd/entire-sem
53	
54	# 2. CBM competitor — required for the head-to-head `bench.py` (the aggregate
55	#    report is entire-sem vs CBM vs naive). Download the binary only; do NOT run
56	#    its install.sh, which rewrites your agent (Claude/Codex/...) MCP configs.
57	#    Indexing + graph export are scripted via `codebase-memory-mcp cli`.
58	curl -fsSL -o cbm.tgz \
59	  https://github.com/DeusData/codebase-memory-mcp/releases/download/v0.8.1/codebase-memory-mcp-darwin-arm64.tar.gz
60	tar xzf cbm.tgz && export GRAPHMARK_CBM=$PWD/codebase-memory-mcp
61	
62	# 3. Point the harness at them and run the pinned corpus.
63	export GRAPHMARK_ORACLE=/tmp/graphmark-bin/oracle
64	export GRAPHMARK_ENTIRE_SEM=/tmp/graphmark-bin/entire-sem
65	python3 bench.py            # clones repos.json at pinned refs, scores, writes results/
66	
67	# Held-out validation set (the anti-overfitting proof in results-heldout/):
68	python3 bench.py --manifest repos-heldout.json --out results-heldout
69	
70	# Single repo, single system — the only CBM-free path (no GRAPHMARK_CBM needed):
71	python3 run.py corpus/mux --system entire-sem
72	```
73	
74	`repos.json` pins each repository to a tag; `bench.py` records the resolved SHA.
75	Cloned sources live under `corpus/` (gitignored). Results land in `results/`.
76	
77	## Metrics
78	
79	Precision / recall / F1 of each system vs the oracle, for:
80	- **symbol inventory** — declared functions + methods,
81	- **call graph (all)** — every caller→callee edge the system emits,
82	- **call graph (exact-only)** — edges the system marks as confidently resolved,
83	  scored against the *full* oracle call set. Recall (and therefore F1) is
84	  intentionally a floor here: it measures how much of the true call graph the
85	  high-confidence subset alone covers, so a low exact-only F1 is expected and is
86	  not a quality defect — read it as precision-of-confident-edges, not coverage.
87	
88	Micro-average pools counts across repos; macro-average means the per-repo scores.
89	
90	## Current results (17 pinned Go repos; `ulid` excluded — incomplete oracle)
91	
92	Aggregate F1 (micro / macro), corpus and held-out, vs the competitor
93	(codebase-memory-mcp) and the naive floor:
94	
95	| metric | entire-sem (corpus) | CBM (corpus) | entire-sem (held-out) | CBM (held-out) |
96	|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
97	| symbol inventory | **1.000 / 1.000** | 0.920 / 0.937 | **1.000 / 1.000** | 0.986 / 0.980 |
98	| call graph (all)  | **0.781 / 0.826** | 0.618 / 0.722 | **0.949 / 0.954** | 0.933 / 0.926 |
99	
100	**entire-sem wins both metrics on both sets.**
101	
102	- **Symbol inventory — entire-sem complete, CBM not.** P/R 1.000, **15/17**
103	  corpus / **4/7** held-out, **0 losses**; with `(file, line)` identity ~1.0 is
104	  the expected bar for any competent parser, so the real signal is CBM trailing
105	  it at 0.92 / 0.99 (declarations it never emits).
106	- **Call graph — entire-sem ahead**, at high precision (P 0.942 corpus / 0.981
107	  held-out). Per-repo it wins **14/17** corpus (CBM wins cobra by 0.008, jwt by
108	  0.065) and **5/7** held-out (0 losses). The held-out set (7 repos never used
109	  while tuning the resolver) is the proof this generalizes rather than overfits.
110	
111	**Honest caveats** (call graph): the aggregate gap is **corpus-dependent** —
112	driven by method-heavy repos where type/scope resolution matters most (pflag
113	+0.59, errors +0.22, websocket +0.17). On the *easy* held-out repos the gap is
114	small (+0.016 micro) and the naive floor nearly ties. The **symbol** win is robust
115	everywhere. entire-sem also does this **without compiling the code**, so it
116	generalizes to languages where no compiler/LSP exists — but **CBM indexes faster**
117	(pure C), so this is an accuracy result, not a speed one.
118	
119	This result was reached by *improving entire-sem* (two general Go call-resolution
120	tiers: same-package, and unique-method-name) — see the entire-sem repo. It then
121	survived an **adversarial audit**: the oracle is genuinely stricter than the tool
122	under test, the comparison is symmetric and reproduces byte-for-byte, and one real
123	precision bug the audit found (the method-name fallback firing on imported-package
124	calls like `json.Marshal`) was fixed before publishing these numbers.
125	
126	Four fairness controls applied symmetrically to every tool: `_test.go` exclusion;
127	the **compiled-file set** (score only files the single-build compiler actually
128	compiled, so build-tagged code isn't counted against a tool — this *also* helps
129	CBM); CBM run at full strength (Function+Method label union, Hybrid LSP active);
130	and repos with incomplete compiler ground truth excluded by a fixed rule.
131	
132	## Honest limitations
133	
134	- **Go, TypeScript, Python, and Rust.** Each language has its own ground-truth
135	  oracle: Go (`go/types`), TypeScript (`oracle-ts/`, ts-morph + the TS type
136	  checker), Python (`oracle-py/`, jedi), and Rust (`oracle-rust-rustc/`, rustc
137	  HIR). Run e.g. TS with `python3 bench.py --manifest repos-ts.json --out
138	  results-ts` (and `bench_tasks.py` for the Tasks matrix).
139	- **Oracle completeness** depends on the repo type-checking cleanly; `bench.py`
140	  warns on load errors and excludes the repo. For TS, `install_deps` stages
141	  `node_modules` after clone so dependency types resolve (the analogue of Go's
142	  module cache).
143	- The `naive` symbol column reuses the compiler's own declarations, so it is 1.0
144	  by construction — ignore it; the real symbol number is entire-sem's. Ignore the
145	  `naive` **call graph (exact-only)** column for the same reason: naive has no
146	  confidence tier, so it reuses its all-calls set as "exact", which makes that
147	  number higher than the real tools' exact-only scores but not comparable to them.
148	- This measures **graph fidelity**, not end-to-end agent task success — a
149	  separate, complementary axis covered by the `competitive-eval/` Tasks suite in
150	  this repo.
151	
152	## Roadmap
153	
154	- [x] `CBM` (codebase-memory-mcp) head-to-head on the same oracle.
155	- [ ] Scale the corpus (more + larger repos) for statistical weight.
156	- [x] Per-language oracles: **TypeScript** (ts-morph + TS type checker),
157	  **Python** (jedi), and **Rust** (rustc HIR) live in both matrices; the
158	  framework is language-agnostic past `oracle_command`.
159	- [ ] Efficiency axis (index wall-time, peak RSS, output size) alongside accuracy.
160	- [ ] Agent-task axis: does the brain measurably help an agent finish a task.
161

1	# agentic-swebench — does the graph help an agent fix real bugs?
2	
3	The **third GraphMark suite**, measuring **downstream agentic value**: does giving a coding
4	agent the entire-graph code-graph tool change how often, and how cheaply, it resolves real
5	GitHub issues? It complements the other two suites — **Fidelity** scores whether the graph is
6	*correct* (compiler oracle); **Tasks** (`competitive-eval/`) scores whether the graph is *useful
7	for retrieval*; this suite scores whether the graph is *useful to an agent solving a task end
8	to end*, graded by the **official SWE-bench harness** (the real project test suites), not by any
9	tool's own output.
10	
11	## Why this design
12	
13	Per-lookup token savings (a graph query vs a file-read sweep) are real but don't tell you whether
14	an agent, over a whole task, resolves more bugs or spends fewer tokens. The only honest way to
15	know is to run the same agent on the same real tasks **with and without** the tool and grade the
16	patches by the project's own tests. So:
17	
18	- **Tasks are real:** the [SWE-bench Multilingual](https://www.swebench.com) dataset (300 GitHub
19	  issues across C, C++, Go, Java, JS, PHP, Ruby, Rust, TS). A 30-task, 3–4-per-language stratified
20	  pilot (`tasks/pilot_tasks.json`, built by `tools/stratify.py`) is the fast signal; the full 300
21	  is the headline.
22	- **Grading is tool-independent:** the official `swebench` Docker harness applies the agent's
23	  patch and runs the instance's real `FAIL_TO_PASS` + `PASS_TO_PASS` tests. `resolved` means the
24	  tests genuinely pass. No tool grades itself.
25	- **The only difference between arms is the graph.** Same agent, same model, same prompt scaffold,
26	  same task. The treated arm additionally gets a `graph-query` tool over a prebuilt entire-graph
27	  dump of the repo at `base_commit`; the baseline arm does not. Everything else is identical
28	  (verified by diffing the two configs — the only deltas are the graph instruction block, the
29	  graph mount, and the graph-tool injection).
30	
31	## Systems
32	
33	| system | what it is |
34	|---|---|
35	| `baseline` | the agent with normal tools only (read / search / edit / run tests) |
36	| `treated` | identical, **plus** `graph-query` over the repo's entire-graph dump |
37	| `graph-query` | the treated arm's tool: `def`/`show` (symbol + its source), `callers`/`callees` (impact), `symbols`/`file` (locate), `stats`. Returns the symbol's actual source so the agent views code without a separate file read. |
38	| *oracle* | the official swebench test suites (the rubric — real pass/fail, not a competitor) |
39	
40	Two agent harnesses are supported, answering different questions:
41	- **subscription** (`tools/run_cc_one.sh`): the agent is Claude Code headless (`claude -p`, no API
42	  key). Baseline is *strong* (Claude Code has efficient built-in navigation), so this is a
43	  conservative test — the graph's benefit is understated.
44	- **official** (`tools/run_pilot.sh` + mini-swe-agent, needs a key): a *naive* bash agent, the
45	  published-comparable setup. Baseline navigates by grep/cat — closer to what the graph replaces.
46	
47	## Reproduce
48	
49	```sh
50	uv venv .venv --python 3.11   # swebench needs Python >=3.10; pin it (uv fetches 3.11 if absent)
51	uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python datasets swebench tiktoken tabulate
52	.venv/bin/python tools/stratify.py                 # -> tasks/pilot_tasks.json (30-task pilot; default)
53	bash tools/batch_graphs.sh                          # -> graphs/<id>/ (host, free, no LLM; bounded + validated)
54	CC_MODEL=sonnet bash tools/run_matrix.sh            # agent runs, both arms (subscription; or run_pilot.sh + key)
55	bash tools/run_eval_model.sh <model> baseline && bash tools/run_eval_model.sh <model> treated   # official Docker eval
56	.venv/bin/python tools/score_matrix.py              # -> results/matrix_compare.md
57	.venv/bin/python tools/fair_tokens.py <model>       # token comparison (whole-pilot primary)
58	```
59	
60	**Quick 30-task pilot vs full 300.** `tools/stratify.py` with no args writes a **30-task**
61	stratified pilot (3–4 per language) — the fast path to a first result, and what every command
62	above assumes. `tools/stratify.py full` writes all **300** instances for the official run. Start
63	with the 30-pilot to sanity-check the harness cheaply; scale to `full` once it looks right.
64	
65	Graphs are bounded to <200 MB each and completeness-validated at build time
66	(`tools/graph_stats.py`); a `graphs/COMPLETENESS.tsv` manifest discloses per-instance parser
67	coverage. Heavy dirs (`graphs/`, `repo-cache/`, `.venv/`) are gitignored.
68	
69	## Metrics
70	
71	- **resolved%** — official swebench, per arm, per language. The primary outcome.
72	- **tokens** — real tokens (cache_creation + input + output) and **$ cost** (economic ground
73	  truth), whole-pilot as the unbiased primary; a matched-task diagnostic is reported *only* with
74	  its collider caveat (see Limitations).
75	- **graph usage** — how often the agent actually calls the tool (a treatment that isn't used
76	  tells you nothing).
77	
78	## Current results
79	
80	**Pending an approved clean run.** The pre-audit pilot numbers were **discarded** — they were
81	produced by a harness carrying 24 now-fixed bugs (below). No number here is trustworthy until the
82	graphs are rebuilt with the fixed deterministic+validated pipeline and both arms are re-run and
83	re-scored. This section will hold: resolved% (baseline vs treated, per language), the whole-pilot
84	token/$ delta, and the completeness manifest.
85	
86	The one robust result that survives the audit is the **isolated per-lookup** measurement
87	(`tools/measure_sweep.py`): answering the five structural questions for a well-connected symbol
88	costs ~2.3k tokens from the graph vs ~654k reading the referencing files (~283x). That is a
89	per-query fact, **not** a whole-session claim.
90	
91	## Honest limitations
92	
93	In GraphMark tradition (the Fidelity suite documents the `_test.go` fairness bug it caught),
94	here is what a reader must know before trusting a number from this suite. Most were found by a
95	multi-pass adversarial audit of the harness itself:
96	
97	- **Whole-session token savings are not the per-lookup number.** Per-lookup is ~283x; across a
98	  full task the honest whole-pilot figure is far smaller and can even be *negative* on a strong
99	  baseline, because the treated agent often keeps trying (and spending) on hard tasks the baseline
100	  abandons cheaply. Report whole-pilot, not the matched subset.
101	- **The matched-task metric is a collider.** Conditioning on "both arms produced a patch" selects
102	  on an outcome the treatment influences and can flip the sign. It's a diagnostic, never the
103	  headline.
104	- **The subscription baseline is strong.** Claude Code's built-in navigation already minimizes
105	  file reading, so the subscription arm *understates* the graph's benefit. The naive mini-swe-agent
106	  baseline shows more.
107	- **The graph is not a resolved call graph.** entire-graph's `CALLS` edges are a fixed-confidence
108	  (0.62) name-collision heuristic; `callers`/`callees` are representative, not exhaustive, and can
109	  mis-attribute overloaded/common names. `def`/`symbols`/`file` and structural (`IMPORTS`/`DEFINES`)
110	  edges are accurate.
111	- **22/30 pilot graphs are provider-`degraded`/`unsafe`** — the parser can't parse some source
112	  files, so the treated arm is blind wherever a file didn't parse. This is disclosed per-instance
113	  in `graphs/COMPLETENESS.tsv`; it is a coverage gap, not corruption.
114	- **CALLS fan-out is capped** (6 per symbol per direction) to bound graph size; high-degree symbols'
115	  neighbor lists are truncated (deterministically).
116	- **Emulation + small n.** SWE-bench images run under amd64 emulation on Apple Silicon (possible
117	  test flakiness); the pilot is n=30 (~3/language) — treat per-language deltas as directional.
118	- **Patch capture is source-only** (excludes lockfiles / vendor / build / the agent's repro
119	  scripts) and includes new source files; it symmetrically caps resolution on the rare gold patch
120	  that adds a file.
121	
122	## Layout
123	
124	```
125	tools/    the harness: graph build (bounded+validated), graph-query, run + eval + scoring
126	tasks/    pilot_tasks.json — the stratified SWE-bench Multilingual pilot
127	tests/    regression suite (70+ checks; every audit finding has a test that fails on the old code)
128	results/  scored output (populated after an approved clean run)
129	```
130

Oracle mechanism independently confirmed. Compact + clean:
- **Symbol inventory** = every `*ast.FuncDecl` with a name, keyed `(file,line)`; kind `method` if `Recv != nil` else `function`.
- **_test.go exclusion** = `packages.Config{Tests: false}` → test files never loaded (oracle side); harness filters tool side symmetrically.
- **Call truth** = resolve each call ident via `TypesInfo.Uses[id].(*types.Func)`, keep edge only if callee lands on an in-module decl (`funcSite` map) → intra-module scope; stdlib/external dropped.
- **naive** = link caller to *every* in-module decl sharing the callee name (`nameIndex`), no type resolution.
- **Compiled-file set** = `pkg.GoFiles` per package (build-tag-filtered fairness control).

# 🧠 entire-graph

![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue)
![Languages](https://img.shields.io/badge/languages-36%20semantic%20%2B%20149%20inventory-2ea44f)
![Graph](https://img.shields.io/badge/graph-30%20relation%20types-8957e5)
![Local](https://img.shields.io/badge/100%25%20local-no%20egress-brightgreen)
![Deterministic](https://img.shields.io/badge/deterministic-no%20LLM%20·%20no%20vectors-f59e0b)
![Accuracy](https://img.shields.io/badge/accuracy-94%25%20on%2021%20repos-success)
![Plugin](https://img.shields.io/badge/Entire%20CLI-plugin-24292f)

**A deterministic, local-first code graph for coding agents, and the semantic layer behind Entire checkpoints.** entire-graph parses your repository with tree-sitter and answers structural questions (where is this defined, who calls it, what changed at the entity level, what will this break) straight from a persistent knowledge graph of functions, classes, call chains, routes, and cross-service links. No model calls, no embeddings, no network. The same commit always produces the same graph.

It ships as an **Entire CLI plugin**, invoked as `entire graph ...`, and doubles as a local-only semantic provider that streams a machine-readable graph of symbols and relations for downstream tools such as Entire Brain. High-quality tree-sitter parsing across **36 semantic languages** and **149 inventory filetypes**, a **30-relation** graph with stable identity, and agent-ready hybrid search, all from a single plugin binary with zero runtime dependencies beyond git.

```sh
entire graph search   --repo . --query "where is webhook retry handled?"   # 🔍 ranked code for a task
entire graph snapshot --repo . --format ndjson                             # 🕸️  full symbol + relation graph
entire graph diff     --base main --head HEAD                               # 🧬 what changed, at the entity level
entire graph capabilities --json                                           # 🧭 languages + relation types
```

> 🔬 **Accuracy first.** On a frozen 21-repo multi-language board of fixed-answer semantic tasks (definition lookup, call graph, imports, change-impact) scored on real checkouts, entire-graph scored **265/283 (94%)** versus **191/283 (68%)** for the leading tree-sitter code-memory tool. A wrong edge is worse than a missing one, so the graph is built to be right about symbols and impact, not just fast at emitting them.
>
> 🔒 **Security and trust.** entire-graph reads your codebase and writes only to Entire's managed plugin directory. All processing happens 100% locally: no network, no telemetry, no API keys, no grammar downloads at runtime. Your code never leaves your machine. `entire graph doctor --json` reports `no_egress=true`.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Deterministic tool-identifier rename for GraphMark: entire-sem -> entire-graph.

Scope: the SAFE CORE only (root harness, oracle, docs, tests, top manifest,
current top-level results). Excludes competitive-eval/ (frozen-evidence path
entanglement -> handled separately) and agentic-swebench/ (already renamed;
its only old-name refs are deliberate historical comments to preserve).

Replaces the tool's machine identifier in three casings. Never touches bare
'sem' / 'semantic' / 'SEM V7' protocol names (they don't contain these tokens),
and the space-form CLI 'entire sem' is handled by hand (README) so historical
comments elsewhere stay intact.
"""
import os, re, subprocess, sys

GM = "/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-suhaan-devenv/7e3deab1-a028-46d5-9bf1-3318de93a0b6/scratchpad/graphmark"
os.chdir(GM)

SUBS = [
    ("entire-sem", "entire-graph"),
    ("entire_sem", "entire_graph"),
    ("ENTIRE_SEM", "ENTIRE_GRAPH"),
]

# Files that contain a hyphen/underscore/UPPER tool token (NOT the space form).
out = subprocess.run(
    ["git", "grep", "-Il", "-e", "entire-sem", "-e", "entire_sem", "-e", "ENTIRE_SEM", "--", "."],
    capture_output=True, text=True,
)
files = [f for f in out.stdout.splitlines() if f]

def excluded(f):
    return f.startswith("competitive-eval/") or f.startswith("agentic-swebench/")

core = sorted(f for f in files if not excluded(f))

# Safety: assert no token is glued to a longer word (semantic-adjacency).
glued = subprocess.run(
    ["git", "grep", "-hoE", r"entire[-_]sem[a-zA-Z]", "--", "."],
    capture_output=True, text=True,
).stdout.strip()
if glued:
    sys.exit(f"ABORT: token glued to longer word:\n{glued}")

total = 0
report = []
for f in core:
    with open(f, "r", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        src = fh.read()
    new = src
    n = 0
    for a, b in SUBS:
        c = new.count(a)
        if c:
            new = new.replace(a, b)
            n += c
    if new != src:
        with open(f, "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
            fh.write(new)
        report.append((n, f))
        total += n

print(f"CORE files changed: {len(report)}  |  total token replacements: {total}\n")
for n, f in sorted(report, reverse=True):
    print(f"  {n:5d}  {f}")

Confidence is a per-TYPE constant here (CALLS=0.62, IMPORTS=0.8, DEFINES/CONTAINS=1.0,
HANDLES_ROUTE=0.7), so a confidence threshold can only keep-ALL or drop-ALL CALLS —

that both bounds size and keeps the feature is CALLS fan-out capping.

  * for CALLS, keep at most CAP_OUT per SOURCE symbol — a HARD fan-out cap applied REGARDLESS

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Regression: the CAP_IN (incoming CALLS) cap must keep a target's HIGHEST-confidence callers,
not whichever sources happen to sort first by from_id.

Audit finding (calls-not-fixed-062): CALLS confidence is GRADED, not a fixed 0.62. The old CAP_IN
loop iterated sources in from_id order and filled the per-target budget first-come, so a
low-confidence caller with a small from_id could evict a genuine high-confidence resolved caller of
the same popular target. This test builds exactly that situation and asserts the high-confidence
callers survive. It FAILS on the old source-order code and PASSES on the confidence-preferring code.
"""
import subprocess, json, sys, os

HERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
FILTER = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(HERE), "tools", "filter_edges.py")  # suite/tools/filter_edges.py

# One popular target T with 8 incoming callers (CAP_IN defaults to 6, so 2 must be dropped).
# The 6 LOW-confidence callers sort FIRST by from_id (F0..F5); the 2 HIGH-confidence callers
# sort LAST (F6, F7). Old code (from_id order) keeps F0..F5 and drops the 0.86 edges; the
# confidence-preferring code must keep the two 0.86 edges.
edges = []
for i in range(6):
    edges.append({"record_type": "relation", "from_id": f"F{i}", "to_id": "T", "type": "CALLS", "confidence": 0.62})
for i in (6, 7):
    edges.append({"record_type": "relation", "from_id": f"F{i}", "to_id": "T", "type": "CALLS", "confidence": 0.86})


def run(order):
    return subprocess.run([sys.executable, FILTER],
                          input="\n".join(json.dumps(e) for e in order),
                          capture_output=True, text=True).stdout


def kept_from_ids(out):
    ids = set()
    for line in out.splitlines():
        line = line.strip()
        if not line:
            continue
        o = json.loads(line)
        if o.get("type") == "CALLS" and o.get("to_id") == "T":
            ids.add(o["from_id"])
    return ids


out = run(edges)
kept = kept_from_ids(out)
assert len(kept) == 6, f"CAP_IN=6 must keep exactly 6 callers of T, kept {len(kept)}: {sorted(kept)}"
assert {"F6", "F7"} <= kept, (
    f"high-confidence (0.86) callers F6/F7 were dropped in favor of low-confidence (0.62) callers "
    f"that sorted first — CAP_IN is not confidence-preferring. kept: {sorted(kept)}"
)

# Determinism: same edge SET in any input order -> byte-identical output (kept property).
assert run(edges) == run(list(reversed(edges))), "CAP_IN output not byte-identical across input orders"

print("PASS filter_edges CAP_IN keeps highest-confidence callers")

# Run the agentic-swebench regression suite. These tests are standalone scripts (each asserts and
# prints PASS / exits nonzero on failure) rather than pytest cases — pytest.ini excludes this dir —

for t in "$HERE"/test_*.py; do

    echo "FAILED: $(basename "$t")" >&2
    rc=1
  fi
done
[ "$rc" -eq 0 ] && echo "ALL agentic-swebench TESTS PASSED" || echo "SOME agentic-swebench TESTS FAILED" >&2
exit "$rc"

input.content:
## What

An integrity + correctness audit of **suite 3 (`agentic-swebench`)** — the arm that measures
whether giving a coding agent an entire-graph code-graph tool changes how often / how cheaply it
resolves real SWE-bench Multilingual issues — plus fixes for every confirmed finding.

**Headline: no win-manufacturing cheat.** The two arms differ only by the graph (verified: the
graph-tool note is appended to the treated prompt only; both arms submit all instances, no
resample, grading is the official swebench harness). Resolution is a genuine **27/30 tie** and the
token deltas are real. The issues found are about **honesty/accuracy of the claims** and one
**graph-quality bug** — not a rigged result. Fixed here so the harness's own disclosures match what
it actually does.

## Findings fixed

**Tool description was false, and it drove a real bug**
- entire-graph's `CALLS` edges were described as a "fixed-confidence (0.62) name-collision
  heuristic" in the README, `filter_edges.py`, and `build_graph.sh`. The tool actually emits a
  **graded** confidence cascade (~0.92 same-file → 0.86 import → 0.80 same-package/dir → 0.68–0.64
  unique-name → ~0.55–0.62 ambiguous), verified against `entire-graph/internal/sem/provider.go`.
- The false "uniform 0.62" premise justified a confidence-**blind** incoming-call cap: `CAP_IN`
  kept whichever callers sorted first by `from_id`, so a 0.62 caller could evict a genuine 0.86
  caller of the same popular symbol. `CAP_IN` is now confidence-preserving (keeps each target's
  highest-confidence callers, still deterministic and bounded). New
  `test_filter_edges_confidence.py` fails on the old code and passes on the new.

**Eval methodology was mislabeled**
- `run_eval_model.sh` could only grade raw `preds.json`, so the "cleaned + `git apply --check`-validated
  (v2)" methodology the harness advertises — and `score_matrix`'s `v2 > clean > raw` preference —
  was unreachable. It now takes a `[raw|clean|v2]` variant with the matching `run_id` suffix.
- `score_matrix.py` hard-coded "(v2)" in the report header regardless of what was scored;
  `matrix_compare.md` prose said "(v2)" while its own table said `raw`. The methodology line is now
  derived from the suffix actually scored.

**Token disclosures**
- The rationale for excluding `cache_read` was stated backwards: excluding it (the `real` headline)
  is the *more* treated-favorable metric (real Δ −13 % vs total Δ −9 %), so `total` and `$ cost` are
  the conservative checks. Corrected in `score_matrix.py` and `fair_tokens.py`.
- Turn-capped (`error_max_turns`) runs have tokens/`$` censored at the cap and mildly under-count the
  arm that caps more; per-arm counts are now disclosed.

**Results ↔ README contradiction**
- README and `results/.gitkeep` said results were "pending / discarded / nothing trustworthy" while
  a full scored report + 180 result files were committed. They now describe the retained
  subscription-mode sonnet pilot honestly (raw eval, 27/30 tie, caveats) and note the official clean
  run is still pending.

**CI gap**
- The suite-3 tests are standalone scripts (excluded from `pytest`), so their streaming/RSS,
  determinism, confidence-cap, and completeness guards had **no CI coverage**. Added a runner and
  wired it into `ci.yml`.

## Testing

`bash agentic-swebench/tests/run_tests.sh` — all invariants pass (graph-query streaming/RSS,
filter determinism + newline safety, the new confidence-cap test, graph_stats completeness). The
root `pytest` suite is unaffected (all changes are under `agentic-swebench/` + the CI step).

## Scope

Analysis-only where it should be: no committed result *numbers* were altered (the token/resolution
figures stand); only misleading *labels* and the graph-build code were changed. The behavioral
`CAP_IN` change improves graph fidelity (keeps resolved calls over name-collision noise) and is
disclosed accurately.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Run ONE pilot task with Claude Code headless (subscription auth, no API key).
# Usage: run_cc_one.sh <baseline|treated> <instance_id>
# Produces: results/<arm>/<iid>/{patch.diff, cc_out.json}
set -uo pipefail
SUITE="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)"   # suite root = parent of tools/
cd "$SUITE"
PY="$SUITE/.venv/bin/python"; [ -x "$PY" ] || PY=python3
arm="${1:?arm}"; iid="${2:?instance_id}"
MODEL="${CC_MODEL:-sonnet}"
MAXTURNS="${CC_MAX_TURNS:-50}"
MODELDIR="${MODEL//\//_}"

# Treated arm REQUIRES a prebuilt graph. While the graph build is still running, a treated task
# whose graph isn't ready yet must NOT run graph-less (that silently makes the arm identical to
# baseline = unfair numbers). Skip WITHOUT writing cc_out.json so run_matrix's idempotency re-runs
# it on a later pass once the graph exists.
if [ "$arm" = treated ] && [ ! -s "$SUITE/graphs/$iid/graph.edges.ndjson" ]; then
  echo "[$iid/treated] SKIP: graph not built yet (will retry next pass)"
  exit 0
fi

read -r repo commit < <("$PY" -c "
import json;d={i['instance_id']:i for i in json.load(open('$SUITE/tasks/pilot_tasks.json'))['instances']}
r=d['$iid'];print(r['repo'],r['base_commit'])")
cache="$SUITE/repo-cache/$(echo "$repo" | tr '/' '__')"
wt="$SUITE/checkouts/$MODELDIR/$arm/$iid"
out="$SUITE/results/$MODELDIR/$arm/$iid"; mkdir -p "$out"

# serialize git-worktree ops on the SAME cache repo (portable mkdir lock; concurrency-safe)
mkdir -p "$SUITE/.locks"
lockdir="$SUITE/.locks/$(basename "$cache").wt.lock"
_lock(){ local t=0; until mkdir "$lockdir" 2>/dev/null; do sleep 0.2; t=$((t+1)); [ $t -gt 600 ] && break; done; }
_unlock(){ rmdir "$lockdir" 2>/dev/null || true; }

# fresh detached worktree at base_commit
_lock
git -C "$cache" worktree remove --force "$wt" 2>/dev/null || true

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Drive the per-model agentic-swebench matrix: haiku(30) + sonnet(20) + opus(10), both arms.
# Models SEQUENTIAL (spare the shared subscription); within a (model,arm), tasks run at CONC
# concurrency; idempotent (skip a completed run: cc_out.json + cost>0 + not is_error).
set -uo pipefail
AS="/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-suhaan-devenv/7e3deab1-a028-46d5-9bf1-3318de93a0b6/scratchpad/graphmark/agentic-swebench"
cd "$AS"
export ENTIRE_GRAPH=/tmp/graphmark-bin/entire-graph
PY="$AS/.venv/bin/python"
CONC="${CONC:-4}"
export CC_MAX_TURNS="${CC_MAX_TURNS:-50}"
export CC_TIMEOUT="${CC_TIMEOUT:-1200}"
PROG="$AS/drive_progress.txt"
log(){ echo "[$(date '+%H:%M:%S')] $*" | tee -a "$PROG"; }

run_one(){
  local model="$1" arm="$2" iid="$3"
  local out="$AS/results/$model/$arm/$iid/cc_out.json"
  if [ -s "$out" ] && "$PY" -c "import json,sys;d=json.load(open('$out'));sys.exit(0 if (d.get('total_cost_usd',0) or 0)>0 and not d.get('is_error') else 1)" 2>/dev/null; then
    echo "[skip] $model/$arm/$iid (already complete)"; return 0
  fi
  CC_MODEL="$model" bash "$AS/tools/run_cc_one.sh" "$arm" "$iid" 2>&1 | tail -1
}
export -f run_one; export AS PY

for spec in "haiku:haiku" "sonnet:sonnet" "opus:opus"; do
  model="${spec%%:*}"; key="${spec##*:}"
  iids=$("$PY" -c "import json;print(' '.join(json.load(open('/tmp/subsets.json'))['$key']))")
  n=$(echo $iids | wc -w | tr -d ' ')

content.text:
Got the concrete reason. Failures are almost all `E_PARSE_ERROR` — tree-sitter hit a file it couldn't parse. entire-graph is pure tree-sitter (no compiler), so any file with syntax the grammar can't handle → one partial-failure → the whole graph is labeled `degraded` (binary: **≥1 fail = degraded**, 0 = ok).

**Why it's near-universal (25/30):** real repos almost always contain ≥1 unparseable file. Concrete:

# entire-graph parse-failure root-cause analysis

## 1. Exact mechanism that flags a file `E_PARSE_ERROR`

The check is **binary, threshold-free**, driven by tree-sitter's own error-recovery nodes.

- Core: `parser.go:324` — after a successful parse + entity walk, `if root.HasError()` sets `ParseStatus{ParseError: true, Code: "E_PARSE_ERROR", ...}` (`parser.go:325`). `root.HasError()` is true if the root **or any descendant** is an `ERROR` or `MISSING` node. There is **no threshold** — one malformed construct anywhere in the file flags the entire file.
- The detail string is built by `collectParseErrorDetails` (`parser.go:338-369`), which walks for the first 5 nodes where `node.IsError() || node.IsMissing()` (`parser.go:348`).
- Distinct earlier branch (`parser.go:264-275`): if `ParseCtx` returns `err != nil`, or `root == nil`/`IsNull` (a total parse failure, not error-recovery), it returns `E_PARSE_ERROR` — unless `ctx.Err() != nil`, in which case it becomes `E_PARSE_TIMEOUT` (`parser.go:269-272`).
- YAML has its own identical `HasError()` branch at `parser.go:276-281`. Groovy bypasses tree-sitter entirely and hard-codes `E_PARSE_ERROR` from its structural parser (`groovy.go:64`).

Key nuance for severity: **`E_PARSE_ERROR` still emits partial symbols.** The error branch does not `continue`/return early — it appends the failure (`provider.go:876-883`) then falls through to emit the file record and whatever entities tree-sitter's error recovery produced (`provider.go:884-907`). So `E_PARSE_ERROR` = "degraded extraction," not "file dropped." By contrast `E_PARSE_TIMEOUT` returns `nil` entities (`parser.go:274`), so a timeout drops all symbols for that file.

**How one failure poisons the repo label:** `completenessLevel` (`provider.go:15777-15786`) returns `ok` only when `failures == 0`; `unsafe` when `failures*4 > files` (>25%); otherwise `degraded`. So a single `E_PARSE_ERROR` on 1 file out of thousands flips the whole repo from `ok` to `degraded`. That fully explains "many repos with just 1 failure" being labeled degraded — the label is maximally sensitive.

## 2. Failure categories — FIXABLE vs INHERENT

**(a) 5s timeout on huge files (`E_PARSE_TIMEOUT`) — PARTIALLY FIXABLE, but not via CLI today.**
- Timeout is a hardcoded `const treeSitterParseTimeout = 5 * time.Second` (`parser.go:140`), applied at `parser.go:245`. It is **not** wired to any option or flag — no override exists (see §3). Raising it is a one-line change but currently requires a recompile.
- Separately, files above `defaultMaxParseBytes = 4 MiB` (`provider.go:34`) never reach the parser at all; they get `E_FILE_TOO_LARGE` (`provider.go:815-831`). This cap *is* an option field (`MaxParseBytes`, `provider.go:298`) but is also not CLI-exposed for snapshot/symbols/edges.
- Verdict: genuinely huge/pathological files that blow 5s are largely inherent to a single-threaded parse, but the knob being hardcoded means some timeouts are artificially induced and trivially recoverable by raising the const. Low expected volume.

**(b) Macro-heavy C (`E_PARSE_ERROR` on .c/.h — micropython 544, redis 119) — MIXED: a masking gap that is *partly* fixable, but with an inherent ceiling.**
- entire-graph already invests heavily here: `maskCUnsupportedSyntax` (`parser.go:1284`, ~600 lines to ~1897) runs a preprocessor-skip-stack, blanks `#…` directives incl. line continuations and multiline block comments (`parser.go:1290-1313`), rewrites Postgres `CATALOG(...)` structs (`parser.go:1319-1329`), file-scope statement macros (`parser.go:1330-1340`), control-iterator macros like `list_for_each` → `for(;;)` (`parser.go:1341-1360`), and `__attribute__` (`parser.go:1361+`). C++ (`parser.go:1897`) and Objective-C (`parser.go:2903`) have their own masks.
- This is textbook whack-a-mole: each new macro idiom (MicroPython's `MP_DEFINE_CONST_*` X-macros, Redis's command tables) is a *new* mask rule. Some fraction is fixable by extending the mask; but because there is **no preprocessor** and macros can expand to arbitrary token soup, a residual set is **inherent** to syntax-only parsing. The code comments themselves frame masking as an ongoing best-effort (e.g. Groovy note at `parser.go:184-190`, TS/Flow notes at `parser.go:171-179`).
- Verdict: incrementally fixable at the margin, asymptotically inherent.

**(c) Malformed test fixtures (babel's 3172 failures, "mostly .js") — INHERENT, and largely a *selection* problem, not a parser problem.**
- entire-graph does **not exclude test or fixture directories.** `isVendoredScanDir` (`provider.go:8274-8289`) skips only `.git/node_modules/vendor/.next/third_party/Pods/…`; `isAmbiguousVendoredDirName` (`provider.go:8298-8303`) adds `build/dist/external/deps`. Nothing matches `test/`, `tests/`, `fixtures/`, `__fixtures__/`. So babel's `packages/*/test/fixtures/**/*.js` — files that are *intentionally* syntactically invalid to exercise the parser's error recovery — are parsed as ordinary source and every one trips `HasError()` → `E_PARSE_ERROR`. This single class almost certainly dominates babel's 3172.
- Verdict: no parser can accept these (they are invalid by construction), so the parse failure is inherent/correct. The *fix* is exclusion (route them out via `--ignore-file`, or a fixture-dir heuristic), not parser work.

**(d) Minified/bundled (`E_MINIFIED`) — correctly skipped.**
- Detected by `looksMinified` (`similarity.go:195-214`): a file is minified only when >70% of bytes (`minMinifiedOverlongByteFraction = 0.7`, `similarity.go:189`) live on lines >5000 bytes (`maxMinifiedLineLen = 5000`, `similarity.go:186`). Calibrated against TypeScript's `scanner.ts` data-literal false-positive (`similarity.go:172-183`). Handled at `provider.go:839-856`: emits a file record, skips symbol parsing, records `E_MINIFIED` warning. This is deliberate and correct — not a bug.

## 3. Existing knobs (with file:line)

| Knob | Where | CLI-exposed? |
|---|---|---|
| `--ignore-file` / `--include-file` | `root.go:310-321` → `ProviderSnapshotOptions.IgnoreFiles/IncludeFiles` (`root.go:206-207`); gitignore-syntax matcher `ignore.go:35-177`; root `.gitignore` auto-loaded `ignore.go:37` | **Yes** |
| `--profile full\|fast\|syntax-only` | `root.go:298-303`, `parseProfile` `root.go:268-279`; specs `provider.go:395-400`. Changes relation depth, **not** parse tolerance | **Yes** |
| `--worktree` / `--no-network` / `--progress` | `root.go:304-309` | Yes |
| Per-language masks | 20+ `maskXUnsupportedSyntax` fns, dispatched `parser.go:197-244`; full list `parser.go:398-…` (`maskTypeScript` 398, `maskRust` 482, `maskJava` 621, `maskKotlin` 644, `maskCSharp` 800, `maskC` 1284, `maskCPlusPlus` 1897, `maskObjectiveC` 2903, etc.) | No (compile-time) |
| Parse timeout (5s) | `treeSitterParseTimeout` const `parser.go:140` | **No override — hardcoded** |
| Max parse bytes (4 MiB) | `MaxParseBytes` option `provider.go:298`, default `provider.go:34` | **Not wired** into `parseProviderFlags` (`root.go:281-327`); only `search` has the unrelated `--max-indexed-files`/`--index-all-files` (`search.go:207-213`) |
| `grammar == nil` inventory fallback | `parser.go:192-193` → `fallbackEntities`; language routing table `parser.go` (e.g. `.dockerfile`/`.xml` have no grammar). Never produces a parse-error status (returns empty `ParseStatus{}`) | n/a |

Note the `OnlyFiles` option (`provider.go:291-294`) also exists for selective indexing but is query-time only, not a snapshot CLI flag.

## 4. Honest assessment: fixable-by-parser vs should-be-excluded

Rough split of the failure *mass*:

- **~Majority (dominated by babel's 3172 intentionally-invalid `.js` fixtures): correctly-failing files that should be EXCLUDED, not parsed.** These are not parser defects — the inputs are invalid by design. ## Findings: harness levers for entire-graph parse-failure noise

### 1. How `build_graph.sh` invokes entire-graph

`tools/build_graph.sh:28` and `:37-38` — the two invocations are:
```
$GRAPH symbols --repo "$cache" --format ndjson
$GRAPH edges   --repo "$cache" --format ndjson | filter_edges.py
```
No `--ignore-file`, no `--include-file`, no `--worktree`, no exclusion of any kind is passed. The repo is checked out at `base_commit` (`build_graph.sh:18`).

Because `--worktree` is absent, the provider takes the **HEAD-tree** path: `provider.go:1227` `useHead := !options.Worktree && …` → true. In that path (`provider.go:8172-8214`) the file list comes from `gitutil.ListFiles(repo,"HEAD")` (git-tracked files only), then `filterVendoredPaths` (vendored-name/lockfile/`.map` skip) and `filterIgnoredPaths` (explicit `--ignore-file` globs only). Note the HEAD path uses `loadExplicitIgnoreMatcher` (`provider.go:8174`), which does **not** load `.gitignore` for filtering — only `headIgnoreMatcher` parses root `.gitignore`, and solely to honor vendored-negation (`provider.go:8182`, `8421-8435`). So gitignored files are excluded only incidentally (they're untracked → not listed); a tracked file matching a `.gitignore` rule is still graphed. The worktree path (`provider.go:8216`, `loadWorktreeIgnoreMatcher` at `ignore.go:35-44`) is the only one that actively applies `.gitignore`, and the harness never uses it.

### 2. entire-graph ignore/include semantics + what it skips by default

- Flags parsed at `cli/root.go:310-321`; both `--ignore-file`/`--include-file` are repeatable, resolved relative to `--repo` if not absolute (`ignore.go:54-73`).
- Semantics are **gitignore-style globs** (`ignore.go:136-177`, `globPatternExpression` at `338-366`): supports `*`, `**`, `**/`, `?`, basename-only rules, trailing-`/` directory rules, leading-`/` anchoring, and `!` negation. `--include-file` is a negation list (re-include). This is exactly the mechanism a pre-filter would use.
- Default dir skipping (`provider.go:8274-8316`): unambiguous vendored names only — `.git, node_modules, vendor, .next, third_party/third-party/thirdparty/3rdparty, Pods, Carthage`, nested bundled C runtimes, and ambiguous `build/dist/external/deps` **only when untracked**. Plus lockfiles and `*.map` (`8340-8348`).
- **Test/fixture dirs are NOT skipped.** There is no `test`, `tests`, `testdata`, `fixtures`, `__fixtures__`, or `spec` handling anywhere in the scan path. Committed fixtures (babel's malformed `.js`) are tracked, non-vendored, and get fully parsed → they drive the failures.

### 3. Fixture pollution of `graph-query` — this is a REAL harm to the treated arm

Measured on the shipped `graphs/babel__babel-13928` graph:
- **87.8% of symbols (103,807 / 118,243) come from test/fixture paths**; only 14,436 are real source.
- `graph-query` (`tools/graph-query`) caps output at `GRAPH_CAP=40` (`graph-query:31`). `symbols`/`def`/`callers` do a plain substring/name match with no path filtering (`graph-query:223,229,231,233`). So common identifiers are swamped: `def type` → 5,399 hits (4,791 fixtures); `sourceType` 5,125 (5,119 fixtures); `body` 4,717 (4,659 fixtures); `name` 4,288 (4,098 fixtures). Real definitions get crowded past the 40-row cap and truncated (`graph-query:139-140,254-255`).
- Fairness note: the graph is a treated-arm-only affordance, so this pollution can only **degrade** the treated arm's own tool — it is not a bias against control. Cleaning it improves the treated arm's tool without giving it any task information control lacks (the fixture files remain on disk for both arms to grep). So it is a quality problem, not a symmetry problem — but a real one, not negligible, on fixture-heavy repos.

### 4. How `completeness_level "degraded"` is computed — it is a strict binary

- The label is the **provider's**, read verbatim by the harness: `graph_stats.py:188` `st.get("completeness_level")` from the summary `stats` dict; surfaced (not rejected) at `graph_stats.py:259-262`, and counted in the manifest at `:287-301`.
- Provider rule (`provider.go:15777-15786`):
  ```
  failures==0            -> "ok"
  failures*4 > files     -> "unsafe"   (>25% of files)
  else                   -> "degraded"
  ```

- Crucially, **99.0% of those 3172 failures (3139) are test/fixture files**; only 33 are non-fixture, and a few of those are vendored/generated (`.yarn/releases/yarn-3.1.0.cjs`) — leaving ~30 genuine real-source parse gaps out of ~10k real-source files (~99.7% real coverage). The current binary label hides that entirely.
- The data to do better already sits on disk: the `summary` record carries a top-level `partial_failures` **array with `file_path` per failure** (`provider.go:1208`, `184-190`) plus `stats.files` and `stats.parsed_files` (`167-174`). `graph_stats.integrity()` currently reads only the scalar `stats.partial_failures` count (`graph_stats.py:189`), never the per-file array — so a graded metric needs no provider change, only a new reader in `graph_stats.py`.

---

**Lever A — exclude test/fixture/vendored/generated files from the graph build.**
Add one static gitignore-style glob file (e.g. `tools/graph_exclude.globs` with `**/test/fixtures/**`, `**/__fixtures__/**`, `**/testdata/**`, `**/*.spec.*`, `**/*.test.*`, `.yarn/**`, plus conservative entries) and pass `--ignore-file "$SUITE/tools/graph_exclude.globs"` on **both** invocations at `build_graph.sh:28` and `:37`. Mechanism already works in HEAD mode via `filterIgnoredPaths` (`provider.go:8183`) with full `**` glob support (`ignore.go:338-366`).
- Effort: low (one glob file + two flag additions). Requires rebuilding all graphs and re-running the treated arm (it changes graph content).
- Risk: low-medium — a project with real source under a literally-named `test/`/`spec/` dir could be over-excluded; mitigate by favoring high-precision globs (`fixtures`, `testdata`, `__fixtures__`, `*.spec.*`) over bare `test/`. Bench provider's own `internal/sem/testdata/**` is irrelevant here (only graphed repos matter).
- Fairness: symmetric — the graph is treated-only and the repo files are untouched (both arms still grep every fixture). Must be a single pre-registered filter applied uniformly to every instance (never per-instance tuning), else it becomes score-shopping. Net effect flips fixture-heavy graphs (babel: 3172→~33 failures) toward clean and de-pollutes `graph-query` (removes ~88% of babel symbols).

**Lever B — make the completeness label reflect real-source coverage (reporting-only, safest).**
In `graph_stats.py`, add a reader for the summary's top-level `partial_failures[]` array (already on disk, `provider.go:1208`), classify each `file_path` as fixture/vendored/generated vs real source using the same glob list, and compute `real_source_coverage = 1 − real_failures / (stats.files − excluded_files)`. Emit a graded label (e.g. `degraded` only when real coverage < X%, else `ok*`) and add the coverage number + real-vs-fixture split to `COMPLETENESS.tsv` (`graph_stats.py:277-285`) and the manifest warning (`:297-306`).
- Effort: low, and self-contained to `graph_stats.py` (no provider change, no rebuild).
- Risk: very low — pure disclosure math; no runtime path touched.
- Fairness: zero impact — changes only a reported metric; neither arm's agent sees it. Fully honest and independent of Lever A, so it can ship alone.

Recommendation: B is the honesty fix and is essentially free and risk-free; A additionally improves the treated arm's tool quality but requires a uniform pre-registered filter + full rebuild/re-run. Here's the full sonnet distribution — and it's **not** a uniform −13% shift, it's bimodal:

```
 saved (>5% cheaper): 15 tasks   flat (±5%): 4   cost MORE (>5%): 11
 mean −6.2%  ·  median −4.9%  ·  range −70% … +104%
 quartiles: Q1 −36%  ·  Q2 −5%  ·  Q3 +16%
 buckets: <−50%:6   −50..−20:4   −20..−5:5   ±5:4   +5..+30:6   >+30%:5
```

**The key honest insight:** the **−13% aggregate ≠ the typical task.** Median is only **−5%**. The aggregate is dragged down by a handful of **huge savers on expensive tasks** (token-weighted):
- redis −70% (saved 80k), ruff −51% (45k), immutable −30% (33k), jekyll −61%, axios −63%, three.js −58%

Meanwhile **11/30 tasks cost MORE** with the graph:
- fmt-2310 **+104%**, nlohmann **+55%**, carbon **+51%**, fmt-1683 **+37%**, gin **+33%**

**Pattern in the tails:**
- **Graph wins** on JS / Ruby / Rust / TS navigation-heavy tasks (replaces big file-read sweeps).
- **Graph loses** on **C++** (fmt +37/+104, nlohmann +55) — exactly where the parser is weakest (macro-heavy, most parse failures), so the graph adds prompt+query overhead without paying off.

**Caveats that make it look better than it is:**
- carbon (+51%) and micropython (+14%) treated **hit the turn cap** → their treated tokens are censored/under-counted, so those losses are actually *worse*.
- `real` excludes cache_read (the more treated-favorable metric); on `total` the aggregate is −9.1%.

So: **not "graph saves 13% everywhere"** — it's "graph saves big on ~half the tasks (where it's accurate), costs extra on ~a third (where it's not), and the net is −13% because the wins land on the expensive tasks." Same 27/27 solve rate throughout.

Base directory for this skill: /private/tmp/claude-501/bundled-skills/2.1.201/675d0a6b1e66affcc209b3c520524107/dataviz

# Data Visualization

A chart is **read by people and executed by you**. This skill turns "make it look
good" into a procedure with checks, so the result is right by construction rather
than by taste.

**The method here is design-system-agnostic.** Nothing in the procedure, the form
heuristic, the six checks, or the mark specs is specific to one product. A design
system supplies a small set of *parameters* (its ramps, a categorical order, a
diverging pair, a status palette, a texture, its surfaces, its filter components);
the method consumes them unchanged. A **validated default palette** is the
reference instance, fully specified in `references/palette.md`. To target your
brand, read that file's structure and substitute its values — touch nothing else.

> The single most important habit: **the color part is computable, so compute it.**
> Never eyeball whether a palette is colorblind-safe — run `scripts/validate_palette.js`.

## The procedure — do these in order

Color comes LAST. Most bad charts pick colors first.

1. **Pick the form.** What is the data's job — magnitude, identity, polarity, a
   single headline, change-over-time? The job picks the chart type, and sometimes
   the answer is *not a chart* (a stat tile or hero number). → `references/choosing-a-form.md`
2. **Assign color by the job it does.** Categorical (identity), sequential
   (magnitude), diverging (polarity), or status (state) — each has one rule.
   Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled. → `references/color-formula.md`
3. **VALIDATE the palette — run the script, don't reason about ΔE.**
   `node scripts/validate_palette.js "<hex,hex,…>" --mode light` (relative to
   this skill's base directory — or load it as `<script type="module">` in the
   chart's own page, where it reads
   `data-palette` off `<body>` and logs a `console.table` report). It returns
   pass/fail on the lightness band, chroma floor, adjacent-pair CVD separation,
   and contrast. Fix anything that FAILs before continuing. Re-run for
   `--mode dark` with that mode's surface.
4. **Apply mark specs & spacers.** Thin marks, 4px rounded data-ends anchored to
   the baseline, 2px lines, ≥8px markers, a 2px surface gap between fills (stacked
   segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring on overlapping marks,
   selective direct labels. → `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`
5. **Add the hover layer — by default.** An HTML/SVG chart *is* interactive; ship
   a crosshair+tooltip on line/area and a per-mark hover tooltip on bar/dot/cell.
   The only form that skips it is a bare stat tile with no plot. Hit targets bigger
   than the mark; filters in one row above the charts. → `references/interaction.md`
6. **Final accessibility pass.** For ≥ 2 series a legend is always present and ≤ 4
   are also direct-labeled (a single series needs no legend box — the title names
   it), so identity is never color-alone; a table view exists; dark mode is **selected** — its own
   steps from the same ramps, validated against the dark surface, not an automatic
   flip; texture is available for the CVD/print/forced-colors case.
7. **Render it and look at it.** The validator checks color, not layout — open or
   screenshot the output and eyeball it for label collisions, geometry, and overflow
   before calling it done.

Then check the result against **`references/anti-patterns.md`** — it is the catalog
of what goes wrong. If your chart matches an entry, it's wrong.

## Non-negotiables (true in every design system)

- **Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled.** A 9th series is never a
  generated hue — it folds into "Other," small multiples, or composite encoding.
- **One axis.** Never a dual-axis chart (two y-scales). Two measures of different
  scale → two charts, small multiples, or indexed to a common base. *(This is the
  #1 chart mistake — see anti-patterns.)*
- **Color follows the entity, never its rank.** A filter that changes the series
  count must not repaint the survivors.
- **Sequential = one hue, light→dark. Diverging = two hues + a neutral gray
  midpoint.** Never a rainbow; never a hue at the diverging midpoint.
- **Run the validator before shipping any categorical palette.** CVD ≥ 12 is the
  target; 8–12 is a floor that is legal ONLY with secondary encoding. A contrast WARN
  obligates visible labels or a table view — it is not dismissable.
- **Thin marks; a legend always present for ≥ 2 series (none for one), with
  selective direct labels (never a number on every point); recessive grid/axes.**
- **Text wears text tokens, never the series color** — values, labels, and legends
  stay in primary/secondary/muted ink; a colored mark beside them carries identity.
- **Status colors are reserved** (good/warning/serious/critical) and never reused
  for "series 4"; they ship with an icon + label, never color alone.

## Plugging in a design system

The method is invariant; only these parameters change per system. The reference
instance — every value filled in — is `references/palette.md`.

| Parameter | What the system provides |
|---|---|
| **Ramps** | the hue scales (named steps) the palette draws from |
| **Categorical theme** | the fixed hue order (a named theme); default + alternates |
| **Sequential hue** | the default single hue for magnitude |
| **Diverging pair** | two warm/cool poles + a neutral midpoint |
| **Status palette** | good / warning / serious / critical — steps distinct from categorical |
| **Texture fill** | one directional hand-drawn fill, used at 45° / 135° |
| **Surfaces** | light & dark chart-surface colors (the validator needs these) |
| **Filter controls** | date-range & dimension controls (behavioral spec in `interaction.md`) |

To onboard a new system: fill those rows, feed its ramps to the validator, and let
it snap each slot to the nearest passing step. Structure and rules stay as written.

## Reference files

| File | What it answers |
|------|-----------------|
| `references/choosing-a-form.md` | Which chart type / is it even a chart? |
| `references/color-formula.md` | The four jobs, the six checks, snap-to-passing |
| `references/marks-and-anatomy.md` | Mark specs, spacers, labels, figures, hero number |
| `references/interaction.md` | Tooltips & hover, filters & time ranges |
| `references/components.md` | The pieces a chart is made of — build each in plain HTML |
| `references/anti-patterns.md` | **What goes wrong — check every chart against this** |
| `references/palette.md` | **The reference palette instance** — every parameter, filled in; swap for your brand's |
| `scripts/validate_palette.js` | Runnable six-checks validator (run it; don't eyeball) |

content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme: `prefers-color-scheme` carries the OS preference, and the viewer's toggle stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, which must override the media query in both directions. The robust pattern is token-level: define the palette as custom properties on `:root`, redefine only the tokens under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` — style components through the tokens, never directly inside the media query — then redefine them again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]` and `:root[data-theme="light"]`. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

8	file into memory. Only the (small) symbols file is loaded; edges are always processed in a
9	single streaming pass with constant memory, a cheap substring pre-filter, and early
10	termination once GRAPH_CAP results are found. It returns in well under a second on the
11	bounded (<200 MB) graphs shipped with the harness, and stays constant-memory (no OOM) even
12	if pointed at a multi-GB edges file.
13	
14	Data (env overridable):
15	  GRAPH_SYMBOLS=/root/graph.symbols.ndjson
16	  GRAPH_EDGES=/root/graph.edges.ndjson
17	
18	Usage:
19	  graph-query def <name>            symbol definition(s): file:line kind signature
20	  graph-query symbols <substr>      symbols whose name contains <substr>
21	  graph-query file <path-substr>    outline: symbols defined in matching file(s)
22	  graph-query callers <name>        symbols that call/reference <name>
23	  graph-query callees <name>        symbols that <name> calls/references
24	  graph-query neighbors <name>      callers + callees
25	  graph-query stats                 graph size + languages + edge-type breakdown
26	"""
27	import sys, os, json
28	
29	SYM = os.environ.get("GRAPH_SYMBOLS", "/root/graph.symbols.ndjson")
30	EDG = os.environ.get("GRAPH_EDGES", "/root/graph.edges.ndjson")
31	CAP = int(os.environ.get("GRAPH_CAP", "40"))
32	
33	# Malformed-line accounting so silent data loss is VISIBLE (reported on stderr, never stdout).
34	STATS = {"parse_errors": 0}
35	
36	
37	def _iter_json(path):
38	    """Yield one parsed JSON object per line. Constant memory (never materializes the file)."""
39	    try:
40	        f = open(path)
41	    except FileNotFoundError:
42	        print(f"graph data not found: {path}", file=sys.stderr)
43	        sys.exit(2)
44	    with f:
45	        for line in f:
46	            if not line.strip():
47	                continue
48	            try:
49	                yield json.loads(line)
50	            except Exception:
51	                STATS["parse_errors"] += 1
52	                continue
53	
54	
55	def _load_symbols():
56	    """Load the (small) symbols file once: list of symbols + header. Edges are NOT loaded."""
57	    syms, hdr, summary_langs = [], None, None
58	    for o in _iter_json(SYM):
59	        rt = o.get("record_type")
60	        if rt == "symbol":
61	            syms.append(o)
62	        elif rt == "summary":
63	            summary_langs = o.get("languages")   # `entire graph` zeroes the header; real
64	            #                                      languages live in the summary record
65	        elif hdr is None and "schema_version" in o:
66	            hdr = o
67	    if hdr is not None and summary_langs:
68	        hdr = {**hdr, "languages": summary_langs}
69	    return syms, hdr
70	
71	
72	def _sym_short(s):
73	    return f'{s.get("file_path","?")}:{s.get("start_line","?")}  {s.get("kind","")} {s.get("name","")}'
74	
75	
76	# Repo root the symbols' file_path is relative to. In the treated container the repo is the
77	# cwd (/testbed); override with GRAPH_REPO. Snippets are read from here so `def`/`show` return
78	# the actual source and the agent does NOT need a separate Read (that is where tokens are saved).
79	REPO = os.environ.get("GRAPH_REPO", os.getcwd())
80	SNIPPET_MAX = int(os.environ.get("GRAPH_SNIPPET_LINES", "60"))
81	
82	
83	def _snippet(s):
84	    """Return the symbol's source lines (bounded), read directly from the repo file.
85	
86	    Security: file_path is resolved under REPO and rejected if it escapes REPO — an absolute
87	    path (e.g. /etc/hostname) or ../ traversal must never read out-of-repo content.
88	
89	    Correctness: printed line numbers are always the REAL source line numbers. For symbols
90	    longer than SNIPPET_MAX we show head + tail; the tail lines keep their true (end_line-
91	    relative) numbers and the elision marker is UNNUMBERED, so the agent never edits a
92	    fabricated line number.
93	    """
94	    fp = s.get("file_path")
95	    a = s.get("start_line")
96	    b = s.get("end_line") or a
97	    if not fp or not a:
98	        return None
99	    # Reject path traversal / absolute file_path: the resolved path must stay within REPO.
100	    repo_real = os.path.realpath(REPO)
101	    path = os.path.realpath(os.path.join(repo_real, fp))
102	    if path != repo_real and not path.startswith(repo_real + os.sep):
103	        return None
104	    try:
105	        with open(path, errors="replace") as f:
106	            lines = f.readlines()
107	    except OSError:
108	        return None
109	    a = max(1, int(a)); b = min(len(lines), int(b))
110	    if b < a:
111	        return None
112	    # body = list of (line_number_or_None, text); None marks the unnumbered elision row.
113	    if b - a + 1 > SNIPPET_MAX:      # bound huge symbols: head + tail, with REAL numbers
114	        head_n = SNIPPET_MAX - 10
115	        body = [(a + i, lines[a - 1 + i]) for i in range(head_n)]
116	        body.append((None, f"    … ({b - a + 1 - SNIPPET_MAX} lines elided) …\n"))
117	        for k in range(10):                        # last 10 lines keep their true numbers
118	            idx = b - 10 + k                        # 0-based index into `lines`
119	            body.append((idx + 1, lines[idx]))
120	    else:
121	        body = [(a + i, ln) for i, ln in enumerate(lines[a - 1:b])]
122	    num = "".join(
123	        (f"{n:>6}\t{ln}" if n is not None else f"{'':>6}\t{ln}") for n, ln in body
124	    )
125	    return num
126	
127	
128	def _print_syms(syms, source=False):
129	    if not syms:
130	        print("(none)")
131	        return
132	    for s in syms[:CAP]:
133	        print(_sym_short(s))
134	        if source:
135	            snip = _snippet(s)
136	            if snip:
137	                print(snip.rstrip("\n"))
138	                print()
139	    if len(syms) > CAP:
140	        print(f"... (+{len(syms)-CAP} more; narrow the query)")
141	
142	
143	def _stream_edges(target_ids, by_id, want_callers, want_callees):
144	    """Single streaming pass over the edges file. Constant memory; stops at CAP results.
145	
146	    Every relation line is parsed and matched on from_id/to_id membership in target_ids —
147	    NOT on a name substring. The old name-substring pre-filter was LOSSY: edges reference
148	    symbols by ID, and a symbol's display name can differ from the bytes on the line
149	    (non-ASCII escaping under ensure_ascii, overloaded names, qualified-vs-bare), so callers/
150	    callees were silently undercounted. filter_edges.py bounds every shipped graph to
151	    <200 MB, so a full streaming parse stays well under a second and never OOMs.
152	    """
153	    res, seen = [], set()
154	    try:
155	        f = open(EDG)
156	    except FileNotFoundError:
157	        print(f"graph data not found: {EDG}", file=sys.stderr)
158	        sys.exit(2)
159	    truncated = False
160	    with f:
161	        for line in f:
162	            if not line.strip():
163	                continue
164	            try:
165	                o = json.loads(line)
166	            except Exception:
167	                STATS["parse_errors"] += 1
168	                continue
169	            if o.get("record_type") != "relation":
170	                continue
171	            typ = o.get("type", "REF")
172	            fid = o.get("from_id")
173	            tid = o.get("to_id")
174	            if want_callers and tid in target_ids and fid in by_id:
175	                key = ("<-" + typ, fid)
176	                if key not in seen:
177	                    seen.add(key)
178	                    res.append(("<-" + typ, by_id[fid]))
179	            if want_callees and fid in target_ids and tid in by_id:
180	                key = ("->" + typ, tid)
181	                if key not in seen:
182	                    seen.add(key)
183	                    res.append(("->" + typ, by_id[tid]))
184	            if len(res) >= CAP:
185	                truncated = True
186	                break
187	    return res, truncated
188	
189	
190	def main():
191	    if len(sys.argv) < 2:
192	        print(__doc__)
193	        sys.exit(1)
194	    cmd = sys.argv[1]
195	    arg = sys.argv[2] if len(sys.argv) > 2 else ""
196	
197	    if cmd == "stats":
198	        # stream-count: symbols from the small file, edges + type breakdown in one streaming pass
199	        syms, hdr = _load_symbols()
200	        langs = (hdr or {}).get("languages", [])
201	        n_edges = 0
202	        types = {}
203	        for o in _iter_json(EDG):
204	            if o.get("record_type") != "relation":
205	                continue
206	            n_edges += 1
207	            t = o.get("type", "REF")
208	            types[t] = types.get(t, 0) + 1
209	        tb = " ".join(f"{k}={v}" for k, v in sorted(types.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1]))
210	        print(f"symbols={len(syms)} edges={n_edges} languages={langs}")
211	        if tb:
212	            print(f"edge_types: {tb}")
213	        if STATS["parse_errors"]:
214	            print(f"[graph-query] note: skipped {STATS['parse_errors']} unparseable line(s)",
215	                  file=sys.stderr)
216	        return
217	
218	    syms, _ = _load_symbols()
219	
220	    if cmd == "def":
221	        # def returns the definition WITH its source, so the agent gets the code here and
222	        # does not need a separate Read/cat of the file (this is the token-saving path).
223	        _print_syms([s for s in syms if s.get("name") == arg or s.get("qualified_name") == arg], source=True)
224	    elif cmd == "show":
225	        # explicit source view for a symbol (alias of def's body)
226	        _print_syms([s for s in syms if s.get("name") == arg or s.get("qualified_name") == arg], source=True)
227	    elif cmd == "symbols":
228	        al = arg.lower()
229	        _print_syms([s for s in syms if al in (s.get("name", "") + " " + s.get("qualified_name", "")).lower()])
230	    elif cmd == "file":
231	        _print_syms([s for s in syms if arg in s.get("file_path", "")])
232	    elif cmd in ("callers", "callees", "neighbors"):
233	        targets = [s for s in syms if s.get("name") == arg or s.get("qualified_name") == arg]
234	        # Skip any symbol missing an "id" (malformed provider record): indexing s["id"] would
235	        # otherwise KeyError and take down every callers/callees query.
236	        target_ids = {s["id"] for s in targets if s.get("id")}
237	        if not target_ids:
238	            print(f"no symbol named '{arg}' (try: graph-query symbols {arg})")
239	            return
240	        by_id = {s["id"]: s for s in syms if s.get("id")}
241	        res, truncated = _stream_edges(
242	            target_ids, by_id,
243	            want_callers=cmd in ("callers", "neighbors"),
244	            want_callees=cmd in ("callees", "neighbors"),
245	        )
246	        if STATS["parse_errors"]:
247	            print(f"[graph-query] note: skipped {STATS['parse_errors']} unparseable edge line(s)",
248	                  file=sys.stderr)
249	        if not res:
250	            print("(no edges)")
251	            return
252	        for tag, s in res[:CAP]:
253	            print(f'{tag:<14} {_sym_short(s)}')
254	        if truncated:
255	            print(f"... (showing first {CAP}; more may exist — narrow the query)")
256	    else:
257	        print(__doc__)
258	        sys.exit(1)
259	
260	
261	if __name__ == "__main__":
262	    main()
