content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme: `prefers-color-scheme` carries the OS preference, and the viewer's toggle stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, which must override the media query in both directions. The robust pattern is token-level: define the palette as custom properties on `:root`, redefine only the tokens under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` — style components through the tokens, never directly inside the media query — then redefine them again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]` and `:root[data-theme="light"]`. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

# Reference palette

This is the **reference instance** of the data-viz method: every parameter the
method needs, filled in with a validated default palette. The rest of the skill
is system-agnostic — **to target your brand, substitute this file's values** and
re-run the validator. Nothing else changes.

## How to use these values

Everything below is plain hex. In an HTML chart, **define the slots you use as
CSS custom properties in a local `<style>` block** at the top of the file, then
reference them by role throughout — so the light/dark values swap in one place,
and the chart body is written against roles rather than raw hex:

```css
.viz-root {
  --surface-1:      #fcfcfb;   /* chart surface */
  --text-primary:   #0b0b0b;
  --text-secondary: #52514e;
  --series-1:       #2a78d6;   /* categorical slot 1 */
  /* …only the roles this chart uses */
}
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  .viz-root {
    --surface-1:      #1a1a19;
    --text-primary:   #ffffff;
    --text-secondary: #c3c2b7;
    --series-1:       #3987e5;
  }
}
```

## Categorical palette

Both modes are selected. The dark column is the same eight hues stepped for the
dark surface, not a separate palette:

| Slot | Hue | Light | Dark |
|------|-----|-------|------|
| 1 | blue | `#2a78d6` | `#3987e5` |
| 2 | aqua | `#1baf7a` | `#199e70` |
| 3 | yellow | `#eda100` | `#c98500` |
| 4 | green | `#008300` | `#008300` |
| 5 | violet | `#4a3aa7` | `#9085e9` |
| 6 | red | `#e34948` | `#e66767` |
| 7 | magenta | `#e87ba4` | `#d55181` |
| 8 | orange | `#eb6834` | `#d95926` |

Light-mode worst adjacent CVD ΔE is 24.2 — well clear of the ≥12 target. Three
light-mode slots (aqua, yellow, magenta) sit below 3:1 contrast on the light
surface: the **relief rule** applies (ship visible direct labels or the table
view). The dark steps were chosen for the dark band (OKLCH L ≈ 0.48–0.67, ≥ 3:1
on the dark surface) and validated as a set — worst adjacent ΔE 10.3, the floor
band, so four-plus series lean on direct labels or texture in dark mode too.

The slot **ordering** is the CVD-safety mechanism, not cosmetic — it was derived
by enumerating orderings and picking the one that maximizes the minimum adjacent
ΔE (see `color-formula.md` § Themes). When you swap in your brand's hues, do the
same: run the validator on candidate orderings and keep the best.

## Operating doctrine (the token-saving rules)

1. **Search first — always.** Your first move on any task is one `entire graph search --query "<task>"`. Do **not** grep / find / cat to locate code before you have searched. Exploration is where ~90% of a session's tokens are wasted.
2. **Then narrow, only as needed.** Search exposes concrete identifiers → use at most one `neighbors --symbol X` (for impact) or read the returned line ranges. Don't fan out.
3. **Trust the graph.** Once search or neighbors shows you the function and its source, **edit it**. Do not re-read the whole file or re-grep to "confirm" what the graph already showed — the graph is deterministic.
4. **Never read a whole file to explore.** If you must read, read the line range around the symbol. To understand a type/class, query it — don't open its file.
5. **Impact = one targeted query.** For "what breaks if I change X", use `neighbors --symbol X --relation CALLS --direction in` — not a whole-graph `snapshot`/`edges` dump, and not a repo-wide grep.
6. **Minimise turns.** Token cost is roughly turns × context. Prefer one precise query over three broad ones. Stop discovery once you can defend the edit with a focused hypothesis (ideally a failing test).
7. **Feature-detect before you trust.** If a language might be inventory-only, check `capabilities --json` first — inventory-only files have file records but no semantic relations.

Quick mental model:

```text
locate  →  entire graph search --query "..."          (ranked code + file:line)
impact  →  entire graph neighbors --symbol X ...       (callers/callees of X)
change  →  entire graph diff --base A --head B          (entity-level, with dependents)
ingest  →  entire graph snapshot --format ndjson        (whole graph)
```

---
@AGENTS.md

Based on the search results, here's what I found about the pi-coding-agent with custom providers, OpenAI-compatible configurations, and Fireworks:

## Key Findings

### Custom Provider Configuration
You can register custom providers with baseUrl and/or headers - for example, all Anthropic requests can go through a proxy by calling `pi.registerProvider("anthropic", { baseUrl: "https://proxy.example.com" })`, or add custom headers to OpenAI requests with `pi.registerProvider("openai", { headers: { "X-Custom-Header": "value" } })`.

### OpenAI-Compatible Support
The library auto-detects compatibility settings based on baseUrl for known OpenAI-compatible providers including Cerebras, xAI, Chutes, DeepSeek, NVIDIA NIM, Together AI, and others. It also supports any OpenAI-compatible API like Ollama, vLLM, and LM Studio.

### Fireworks Configuration
Fireworks has an OpenAI-compatible endpoint at https://api.fireworks.ai/inference/v1. The system includes fixes for Fireworks Anthropic-compatible requests to apply session-affinity and unsupported tool-field defaults for custom Fireworks models.

### Headless/Non-Interactive Usage
Credentials come from environment variables (OPENAI_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, OPENROUTER_API_KEY, FIREWORKS_API_KEY, …) or Pi's ~/.pi/agent/auth.json if you've logged in interactively. This allows for headless configuration using environment variables.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Pi coding agent arm (Fireworks OSS models). Mirrors run_3arm.sh semantics:
# same worktree setup, same prompts (baseline vs eg TOOLNOTE), same patch collection.
# Usage: FW_MODEL=<fireworks model id> PI_TAG=<tag> [ARM=base|eg] run_pi_arm.sh <arm> <iid>
# Token accounting: pi --mode json event stream -> tools/pi_tokens.py (per-assistant-message
# usage summed; includes cacheRead/cacheWrite — same 4 components as the claude arms).
set -uo pipefail
SUITE="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)"; cd "$SUITE"
PY="$SUITE/.venv/bin/python"; [ -x "$PY" ] || PY=python3
arm="${1:?arm base|eg}"; iid="${2:?iid}"
FW_MODEL="${FW_MODEL:?fireworks model id}"
TAG="${PI_TAG:?results tag}"
PI_TIMEOUT="${PI_TIMEOUT:-1200}"
EG="${ENTIRE_GRAPH:-/tmp/graphmark-bin/entire-graph-snap20}"
T="$SUITE/tools"
[ -n "${FIREWORKS_API_KEY:-}" ] || { echo "[$iid/$arm] FIREWORKS_API_KEY missing"; exit 1; }

if [ "$arm" = eg ] && [ ! -s "$SUITE/graphs/$iid/graph.edges.ndjson" ]; then
  echo "[$iid/eg] SKIP: no entire-graph dump"; exit 0; fi

read -r repo commit < <("$PY" -c "
import json;d={i['instance_id']:i for i in json.load(open('$SUITE/tasks/pilot_tasks.json'))['instances']}
r=d['$iid'];print(r['repo'],r['base_commit'])")
cache="$SUITE/repo-cache/$(echo "$repo"|tr '/' '__')"
wt="$SUITE/checkouts/$TAG/$arm/$iid"; out="$SUITE/results/$TAG/$arm/$iid"; mkdir -p "$out"

mkdir -p "$SUITE/.locks"; lockdir="$SUITE/.locks/$(basename "$cache").wt.lock"
_lock(){ local t=0; until mkdir "$lockdir" 2>/dev/null; do sleep 0.2; t=$((t+1)); [ $t -gt 600 ]&&break; done; }
_unlock(){ rmdir "$lockdir" 2>/dev/null||true; }
_lock; git -C "$cache" worktree remove --force "$wt" 2>/dev/null||true; rm -rf "$wt"; mkdir -p "$(dirname "$wt")"
git -C "$cache" worktree add --force --detach "$wt" "$commit" >/dev/null 2>&1||{ _unlock;echo "[$iid] wt fail";exit 1; }; _unlock

ps_file="$out/problem.txt"
"$PY" -c "import json;d={i['instance_id']:i for i in json.load(open('$SUITE/tasks/pilot_tasks.json'))['instances']};open('$ps_file','w').write(d['$iid']['problem_statement'])"

TOOLNOTE=""
if [ "$arm" = eg ]; then
  gq="$SUITE/graphs/$iid/eg-q-pi.run"
  cat > "$gq" <<SH
#!/usr/bin/env bash
GQLOG="$out/gq_calls.log" EG="$EG" WT="$wt" GSYM="$SUITE/graphs/$iid/graph.symbols.ndjson" GEDGES="$SUITE/graphs/$iid/graph.edges.ndjson" CACHE="$SUITE/.eg_cache/$iid" EG_SEARCH_LEAN=0 EG_DROP_TESTS=0 EG_LOCATIONS=0 EG_PROFILE=full EG_TIER=2 exec "$T/eg-q" "\$@"
SH
  chmod +x "$gq"
  # IDENTICAL wording to the claude-arm search-only note (fairness)
  TOOLNOTE="

A precomputed code-search tool is available: $gq . Use it to LOCATE the fix BEFORE any grep/find.
Your FIRST action must be ONE search:
  $gq search \"<the bug in one sentence>\"   <-- ranked relevant code (file:line + source)
Then open the top hit's file with your native read tool (pass a line range around the reported
line), make the minimal edit, and STOP. The search top hit is the fix site on most tasks — go
straight there and edit; do NOT re-search or grep to 'confirm'. Reach the edit in as FEW turns as
possible (every turn re-reads your whole context — that is the token cost). Hard rules:
(1) SEARCH FIRST. (2) After search, READ the file directly (line range) and EDIT — do not chain
more searches. (3) NEVER read a whole file to explore; pass a line range. (4) NEVER search outside
this repo. Apply the minimal fix and STOP the moment you can justify it."
fi

PROMPT="You are fixing an issue in the software repository at the current working directory.

<issue>
$(cat "$ps_file")
</issue>

Instructions:
- Make changes ONLY to non-test source files needed to resolve the issue, general and consistent with the codebase.
- Do NOT modify tests, build files, or config.
- Do NOT commit. When finished, just stop — your git working-tree diff is collected as the fix.
- Implement a correct, minimal, general fix.$TOOLNOTE"

echo "[$iid/$arm] pi ($FW_MODEL)…"
( cd "$wt" && exec pi --provider fireworks --model "$FW_MODEL" -p --mode json --no-session \
    "$PROMPT" < /dev/null ) > "$out/pi_out.jsonl" 2> "$out/pi_err.log" &
pi_pid=$!
( sleep "$PI_TIMEOUT"; kill -0 "$pi_pid" 2>/dev/null && { pkill -TERM -P "$pi_pid"; kill -TERM "$pi_pid"; sleep 3; pkill -9 -P "$pi_pid"; kill -9 "$pi_pid"; echo "[$iid/$arm] TIMEOUT"; } ) & wd=$!
wait "$pi_pid" 2>/dev/null; kill "$wd" 2>/dev/null
bash "$SUITE/tools/collect_patch.sh" "$wt" "$out/patch.diff"
"$PY" "$T/pi_tokens.py" "$out/pi_out.jsonl" > "$out/usage.json" 2>/dev/null || echo '{"total":0}' > "$out/usage.json"
tok=$("$PY" -c "import json;print(json.load(open('$out/usage.json'))['total'])" 2>/dev/null||echo '?')
echo "[$iid/$arm] done: patch=$(wc -l <"$out/patch.diff"|tr -d ' ')L tokens=$tok"
_lock; git -C "$cache" worktree remove --force "$wt" 2>/dev/null||rm -rf "$wt"; _unlock

57.8% on what mdoel etc

**57.74% = Claude Sonnet** (`claude -p --model sonnet`, the Claude Code CLI headless agent). Full spec of that number:

| dimension | value |
|---|---|
| **Agent model** | Sonnet (all 3 arms — baseline, cmm, eg — same model) |
| **Agent harness** | `claude -p` headless, max 50 turns, 25-min timeout, `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, no web tools |
| **What's measured** | total tokens per session = input + cache-creation + **cache-read** + output (cache-read dominates — every turn re-reads context) |
| **Savings vs** | no-tool baseline agent, same model/prompt (35.33M baseline tokens over the suite) |
| **Suite** | 23 SWE-bench instances, 10 languages |
| **Runs** | 3× per arm (69 eg + 69 cmm sessions vs baseline denominators) |
| **eg config** | snap20 frozen binary (PR#54 stack) + `--profile full` + tiered output + search-only prompt |
| **cmm** | their static binary, fast index, their 4-verb prompt |

So: **on Sonnet, an agent with entire-graph spends 57.7% fewer tokens than the same Sonnet agent with no tool** (13.38M vs 31.6M effective over 3× means), while the same agent with cmm saves only 36.6%.

Mat's right — repo-level AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md only teaches agents working **on** entire-graph. An agent in a *user's* project never sees it. Four distribution mechanisms, layered:

## 1. Ship a Claude Code **skill** with the plugin (the real fix)
A `SKILL.md` whose description triggers on "find code / where is X / locate the bug" — body = the measured-best prompt + doctrine. Skills auto-load when relevant, so the agent gets the doctrine **in the user's project** with zero setup beyond install. Precedent already exists in the CLI: `entire agent add claude-code --search-skill` installs an "Entire search skill" — same mechanism, new content. And the insider feedback literally asked for this: *"we would need a skill to teach our agents how to use things correctly."*

## 2. `entire enable` / `agent add` drops a pointer into the project's CLAUDE.md
On enable, write `.entire/graph-agent.md` (plugin-managed, updatable) and append one line to the project CLAUDE.md: `@.entire/graph-agent.md`. Import works the same as our repo-level trick, but now in *their* repo. One-line footprint, plugin owns the content.

## 3. Self-teaching CLI output (agent-agnostic — covers Gemini/Codex/Pi too)
- `entire graph` bare → print the agent one-pager (not just usage)
- First search result in a session gets a 1-line footer hint ("read the top hit with a line range and edit; don't re-search")
Agents learn from tool output; this reaches **every** agent brand with no doc plumbing at all.

## 4. (When MCP lands via brain) tool-description carries the doctrine
Tool descriptions are read at discovery time — the prompt travels inside the tool itself.

**Recommended reply to Mat:** repo docs were step 1 (agents working on the repo); step 2 is `--search-skill`-style distribution — plugin installs a skill + CLAUDE.md pointer into the consuming project, plus self-teaching CLI output for non-Claude agents.

content.text:
## Built + shipped: universal agent skill → **PR #56**

**The fix for Mat's problem** — the doctrine now lives in the binary and installs into *consuming* projects, agent-brand-agnostic:
- **`entire graph agent-guide`** — prints the canonical guide (the benchmark-winning search-first block, reworded agent-agnostic: "your file-read tool", full command forms with `--profile full`). Bare `entire graph` help banner points to it → self-teaching output reaches *every* agent.
- **`entire graph init-agents --repo .`** — writes `.entire/graph-agent.md` + upserts a marker-guarded pointer into **AGENTS.md** (the Codex/Gemini/Cursor/Pi convention) and **CLAUDE.md** (with `@`-import). Idempotent, never clobbers, re-run updates in place.
- Tested (content/install/preserve/idempotence), build+vet+tests green, live-smoked. Follow-up noted in PR: wire into `entire enable`/`agent add`.

## Benchmark progress
| suite | status |
|---|---|
| **sonnet 3×** | ✅ DONE — **eg 57.7% vs cmm 36.6% (+21.2pt), all 10 languages, goal met** |
| **opus-10** | 29/30 sessions done — scoring imminent |
| **haiku-30** | baseline 25/30; cmm+eg arms queued |
| **Pi+Fireworks** | 4 model subagents running; early: **kimi-k2.6 requests −63.8%** (177k→64k), gpt-oss smoke **−97%**, glm-5.2 healthy (both arms settling, clean patches) |
| **cmm search-only control** | queued behind the session drain |

Early cross-model signal is exactly what we hoped: the graph's savings are transferring to open-source models on an open-source agent. Full per-model tables land via the subagent notifications.

## Opus + Haiku: savings and "accuracy"

**Savings (vs same-model no-tool baseline):**
| model | eg | cmm | eg edge |

| **Opus** (10 inst) | **52.7%** | 44.9% | +7.8pt |

**Accuracy — the honest answer in two parts:**

1. **Completion proxy (measured, above):** non-empty-patch rate is near-uniform — eg **10/10 opus, 30/30 haiku, 23/23 sonnet**; baseline 10/10, 30/30, 19/20; cmm dropped one opus instance. So **eg's savings are NOT from quitting early** — it finishes with a patch at least as often as both other arms. That was the fairness audit's "rewards quitting" worry: disconfirmed at the completion level.

2. **True resolved% (does the patch pass the instance's tests): not run in these suites.** It needs the per-instance docker test harness — a real build we haven't wired here. Prior measured context from our earlier GraphMark suite-3 work: the graph was **accuracy-neutral on SWE-bench resolution (~0 delta, within noise)** — it's a token lever, not a correctness lever. No reason to expect these runs differ, but that's inference, not measurement for opus/haiku specifically.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Official SWE-bench Multilingual 300 scorer: eg vs cmm vs no-tool baseline (haiku).
Weighted (token-sum) + per-language + winner counts. Uses tools/ml300_langmap.json.
Only instances with a complete arm-triple count toward the three-way comparison;
partial coverage is reported, never hidden."""
import json, os, sys

ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
LANG = json.load(open(f"{ROOT}/tools/ml300_langmap.json"))

def tk(p):
    try:
        u = json.load(open(p))["usage"]
        v = u["input_tokens"]+u.get("cache_creation_input_tokens",0)+u.get("cache_read_input_tokens",0)+u["output_tokens"]
        return v if v > 0 else None
    except Exception:
        return None

iids = [l.strip() for l in open(f"{ROOT}/.elig_ml300.txt") if l.strip()]
rows = []
for iid in iids:
    b = tk(f"{ROOT}/results/ml300base_r1/baseline/{iid}/cc_out.json")
    c = tk(f"{ROOT}/results/ml300cmm_r1/cmm/{iid}/cc_out.json")
    e = tk(f"{ROOT}/results/ml300_r1/eg/{iid}/cc_out.json")
    rows.append((iid, LANG.get(iid, "?"), b, c, e))

full = [r for r in rows if r[2] and r[3] and r[4]]
def wsav(rs, i):
    sb = sum(r[2] for r in rs); sa = sum(r[i] for r in rs)
    return round(100*(sb-sa)/sb, 2) if sb else None

print(f"coverage: baseline {sum(1 for r in rows if r[2])}/300  cmm {sum(1 for r in rows if r[3])}/300  eg {sum(1 for r in rows if r[4])}/300  full-triples {len(full)}")
if full:
    print(f"\nWEIGHTED (full triples, n={len(full)}): cmm {wsav(full,3)}%  |  eg {wsav(full,4)}%  |  gap {round(wsav(full,4)-wsav(full,3),2)}pt")
    ew = sum(1 for _,_,b,c,e in full if 100*(b-e)/b > 100*(b-c)/b + 3)
    cw = sum(1 for _,_,b,c,e in full if 100*(b-c)/b > 100*(b-e)/b + 3)
    print(f"winners: eg {ew} / cmm {cw} / tie {len(full)-ew-cw}")
    print(f"\n{'lang':8s}{'n':>4s}{'cmm%':>9s}{'eg%':>9s}{'gap':>8s}")
    for lang in sorted({r[1] for r in full}):
        lr = [r for r in full if r[1] == lang]
        print(f"{lang:8s}{len(lr):>4d}{wsav(lr,3):>9.1f}{wsav(lr,4):>9.1f}{round(wsav(lr,4)-wsav(lr,3),1):>8.1f}")
if "--json" in sys.argv and full:
    out = {"n": len(full), "cmm_weighted": wsav(full,3), "eg_weighted": wsav(full,4)}
    for lang in sorted({r[1] for r in full}):
        lr = [r for r in full if r[1] == lang]
        out[f"{lang}_gap"] = round(wsav(lr,4)-wsav(lr,3),2)
    print(json.dumps(out))

## SWE-bench Multilingual Leaderboard Status

The SWE-bench Multilingual leaderboard was last updated in July 2026 and currently includes 34 evaluated models.

## Submission Process Using sb-cli

You can submit to the leaderboard using sb-cli, which is a cloud-based evaluation tool. SWE-bench CLI is a command-line tool for interacting with the SWE-bench API.

### Basic Submission Steps

The submission process involves:

1. Creating a pull request to the experiments repository with your submission files
2. Forking the experiments repository and adding your submission files under experiments/multimodal/YOUR_MODEL_NAME/

### Predictions Format

Your predictions file should be a JSON file in one of these formats, either as objects or as a list containing `instance_id`, `model_patch`, and `model_name_or_path` fields.

### Using sb-cli Submit Command

You can submit using the command: sb-cli submit <subset> <split> --predictions_path <path> [options], where the subset can be swe-bench-m, swe-bench_lite, or swe-bench_verified.

### Important Notes

- SWE-bench Multimodal predictions can only be evaluated using sb-cli. You do not need to submit predictions, logs/, or trajs/ for SWE-bench Multimodal
- If you don't have enough quota for the swe-bench-m / test split, you can email the SWE-bench team at support@swebench.com, as they're currently limiting submissions to prevent abuse

input.content:
graphmark · runbook

Run the official SWE-bench Multilingual 300 token benchmark on Opus

Reproduces the haiku-300 measurement (entire-graph 54.9% vs cmm 27.4% savings) with --model opus. Three arms — no-tool baseline, codebase-memory-mcp, entire-graph — 300 instances, 9 languages, ~900 sessions. Everything is restart-safe; rerunning any step skips completed work.

⚠️ Cost & time budget (read first) Opus is ~5–10× haiku per token. The haiku run consumed ~35M baseline-arm tokens alone; expect $1,500–$4,500 total for 900 opus sessions and ~24–48 h wall-clock at concurrency 4–5 (opus generates slower — keep CC_TIMEOUT=2400). Disk: ≥60 GB free (repo caches ~8 GB, graphs ~7 GB, docker headroom if you later run resolved%). Dry-run the pipeline on 10 instances first (step 7).

0Prerequisites

  • claude CLI authenticated (Claude Code; sessions run as claude -p --model opus)
  • Go ≥1.22 + CGO (tree-sitter), git, python3, ~60 GB disk, network (partial clones fetch blobs at worktree time)
  • The graphmark repo (harness lives in agentic-swebench/) and the entire-graph repo
  • cmm reference: the codebase-memory-mcp static binary (their release)
git clone https://github.com/entirehq/graphmark && cd graphmark/agentic-swebench
export AS="$PWD"                      # harness root, used throughout
python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install datasets

1Build the entire-graph binary (main)

Main already contains the full measured stack: test-artifact demotion, gated call-graph vocab bridge, centrality ranking, native tiered output, snippet-crash fix.

git clone https://github.com/entireio/entire-graph && cd entire-graph
go build -o /tmp/graphmark-bin/entire-graph-opus300 ./cmd/entire-graph
go test ./internal/sem/ ./internal/cli/ -count=1        # must be green
cd "$AS"

2Fetch the official dataset

Official set: swe-bench/SWE-bench_Multilingual (Hugging Face, 300 test instances). The harness reads tasks/pilot_tasks.json; the repo already ships tasks/multilingual_300.json, .elig_ml300.txt (300 ids) and tools/ml300_langmap.json — verify or regenerate:

.venv/bin/python - <<'EOF'
from datasets import load_dataset; import json
ds = load_dataset("swe-bench/SWE-bench_Multilingual", split="test")
inst = [dict(r) for r in ds]
json.dump({"instances": inst}, open("tasks/multilingual_300.json","w"))
open(".elig_ml300.txt","w").write("\n".join(r["instance_id"] for r in inst)+"\n")
print(len(inst), "instances")
EOF
# merge into the harness task file (idempotent union; existing entries kept verbatim)
python3 - <<'EOF'
import json
pilot=json.load(open('tasks/pilot_tasks.json')); ml=json.load(open('tasks/multilingual_300.json'))
have={i['instance_id'] for i in pilot['instances']}
pilot['instances'] += [i for i in ml['instances'] if i['instance_id'] not in have]
json.dump(pilot, open('tasks/pilot_tasks.json','w'))
EOF

3Clone the 41 repo caches + verify commits

Naming: repo-cache/<owner>__<name> via tr '/' '__' (what run_3arm.sh computes). Partial clones keep disk small; blobs fetch on demand at worktree-add.

python3 - <<'EOF'
import json, subprocess, os
inst = json.load(open('tasks/multilingual_300.json'))['instances']
repos = sorted({i['repo'] for i in inst})
for r in repos:
    d = "repo-cache/" + r.replace("/", "__")
    if not os.path.isdir(d):
        subprocess.run(["git","clone","--no-checkout","--filter=blob:none",
                        f"https://github.com/{r}.git", d], check=True)
# verify every base_commit resolves; fetch if missing
for i in inst:
    d = "repo-cache/" + i['repo'].replace("/", "__")
    ok = subprocess.run(["git","-C",d,"cat-file","-e",i['base_commit']+"^{commit}"]).returncode==0
    if not ok: subprocess.run(["git","-C",d,"fetch","origin",i['base_commit']])
print("caches ready")
EOF

4Build the 300 graph dumps (eg arm input)

One dump per instance (symbols + edges NDJSON at the instance's commit). The batch driver is parallel across repos, serial within a repo (cache-checkout race), idempotent — rerun it to sweep stragglers.

ENTIRE_GRAPH=/tmp/graphmark-bin/entire-graph-opus300 nohup bash tools/ml300_graphs.sh > .ml300_graphs.log 2&>1 &
# watch:  grep -c OK .ml300_graphs.log ; done marker: "ML300 GRAPH BATCH DONE"
find graphs -name graph.edges.ndjson | wc -l     # target: 300

Disclosure step: tools/graph_stats.py manifest graphs/ — note which languages are inventory-only for the provider; report that beside results.

5Understand the three arms

armtoolpromptneeds
baselinenonefix-the-issue instructions only—
cmmcodebase-memory-mcp (fast index, per-worktree)its 4-verb note (search/def/callers/grep)cmm binary
egentire-graph search via eg-qsearch-only note (one search → read range → edit)graph dumps

Arms share model, turn cap (50), timeout, prompt skeleton, token accounting (input + cache-creation + cache-read + output from the CLI's own usage). Optional fairness control: rerun cmm with SEARCH_ONLY=1 (identical prompt wording) — on sonnet this lifted cmm ~+16 pt and eg still led by ~8.

6Dry run (10 instances) — validate the pipeline

head -10 .elig_ml300.txt > .elig_dry.txt
export CC_MODEL=opus CC_TIMEOUT=2400 ELIG="$AS/.elig_dry.txt"
bash tools/run_multi.sh baseline /bin/true dry300base 1 3
bash tools/run_multi.sh cmm /path/to/codebase-memory-mcp dry300cmm 1 3
ENTIRE_GRAPH=/tmp/graphmark-bin/entire-graph-opus300 SEARCH_ONLY=1 EG_PROFILE=full \
  bash tools/run_multi.sh eg /tmp/graphmark-bin/entire-graph-opus300 dry300 1 3

Check: every session dir has cc_out.json with total_cost_usd>0 and a patch.diff. Extrapolate cost ×30 before committing to the full run.

7Full run — 900 opus sessions

export CC_MODEL=opus CC_TIMEOUT=2400 ELIG="$AS/.elig_ml300.txt"
nohup bash -c '
  bash tools/run_multi.sh baseline /bin/true op300base 1 4
  bash tools/run_multi.sh cmm /path/to/codebase-memory-mcp op300cmm 1 4
  ENTIRE_GRAPH=/tmp/graphmark-bin/entire-graph-opus300 SEARCH_ONLY=1 EG_PROFILE=full \
    bash tools/run_multi.sh eg /tmp/graphmark-bin/entire-graph-opus300 op300 1 4
' > op300.log 2&>1 &
  • Restart-safe: run_multi.sh skips any session whose cc_out.json has cost>0 — rerun the same command after any crash.
  • Progress: find results/op300base_r1 -name cc_out.json | wc -l (same per tag).
  • Don't run graph builds and arms on the same repo concurrently.
  • Retry policy: only sessions with missing/zero-cost output, once, arm-symmetric.

8Score

Point the scorer at the opus tags (env-free edit or sed the tag names in tools/ml300_score.py: ml300base_r1→op300base_r1 etc.), then:

python3 tools/ml300_score.py            # weighted + per-language + winners
python3 tools/ml300_score.py --json     # machine-readable

Report: weighted savings both arms, per-language table (n per language), winner counts, coverage (missing triples disclosed), single-run caveat (per-repo noise ±40–90 pt; language means and the aggregate are the stable readouts). For a variance-hardened claim, repeat arms ×3 and score means.

9Optional — resolved% + leaderboard

The official leaderboard ranks resolved%, not tokens. Patches are already saved, so accuracy is scoreable without re-running agents:

# build predictions from the eg arm
python3 - <<'EOF'
import json,os
preds=[{"instance_id":i,"model_patch":open(f"results/op300_r1/eg/{i}/patch.diff").read(),
        "model_name_or_path":"claude-opus+entire-graph"}
       for i in open(".elig_ml300.txt").read().split()
       if os.path.getsize(f"results/op300_r1/eg/{i}/patch.diff" ) > 0]
json.dump(preds, open("submission_eg_op300.json","w")); print(len(preds))
EOF
# official docker harness (x86 linux recommended; hours)
pip install swebench
python -m swebench.harness.run_evaluation \
  --dataset_name swe-bench/SWE-bench_Multilingual --split test \
  --predictions_path submission_eg_op300.json --max_workers 8 --run_id eg_op300

Then fork SWE-bench/experiments, add evaluation/multilingual/<date>_<name>/ (predictions, logs, results, metadata) and open the PR — see swebench.com/submit.html. Their checklist prefers full per-turn trajectories; claude -p keeps only session summaries, so expect the no-trajectory annotation unless you capture transcripts separately.

10Gotchas we hit (so you don't)

  • Variance: single runs swing ±40–90 pt per repo. Never conclude from one instance; language means + weighted aggregate only. 3× for headline claims.
  • Dirty caches: a leftover modification in a repo cache poisons every graph built from it — git -C repo-cache/X status before building; reset hard if dirty.
  • Trailing newlines in elig files: a missing final newline once concatenated two instance ids.
  • Turn-cap censoring: baseline sessions that hit the 50-turn cap understate baseline tokens → savings are conservative, but name the capped sessions.
  • Blob-less clones need network at worktree-add time.
  • Timeout kills: the watchdog "Terminated" lines in logs are benign cleanup; a real timeout shows TIMEOUT and a zero-cost session (retry it).

Reference — the haiku-300 result this reproduces

armweighted savingsnotes
entire-graph54.9%wins 216/293 instances, 8/9 languages
codebase-memory-mcp27.4%4-verb documented config
baseline0 (definition)~35M tokens total

Opus expectation from the 10-instance pilot: eg 52.7% vs cmm 44.9% — directionally consistent; the 300-run is what makes it citable.

# Entire Graph

**This release is for your agents.**

Entire Graph gives coding agents a precomputed, deterministic map of your codebase — every
function, type, route, and call relationship — so they stop burning your budget on grep-and-read
exploration and go straight to the fix.

On the official **SWE-bench Multilingual** benchmark (300 real issues, 9 languages), an agent with
Entire Graph used **55% fewer tokens** than the same agent without it — roughly **double the
savings of the next-best code-memory tool** — winning 8 of 9 languages, with identical task
completion. 100% local, no network, no model calls, no keys.

## Install (one minute)

```sh
go install github.com/entireio/entire-graph/cmd/entire-graph@latest
entire plugin install "$(go env GOPATH)/bin/entire-graph" --force
```

Then, in any repo your agents work in:

```sh
entire graph init-agents
```

That's it. `init-agents` drops the operating guide into your project's `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md`,
so Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, Cursor, Pi — any agent that reads those files — picks up the
search-first workflow automatically. No config, no MCP server, no daemon.

## What your agents get

| agent workflow | before | with Entire Graph |
|---|---|---|
| **Locate a fix** | grep → open files → grep again (~90% of session tokens) | one `entire graph search` → read a line range → edit |
| **Impact of a change** | repo-wide grep for callers | `entire graph neighbors --symbol X --relation CALLS --direction in` |
| **Review a diff** | file-by-file reading | `entire graph diff` — entity-level changes with dependent counts |

The search understands natural language ("XTRIM trims wrong stream entries"), ranks real
implementation code above tests and docs, bridges vocabulary gaps through the call graph, and
returns budgeted output designed to drop straight into an agent's context.

Want the exact agent instructions? `entire graph agent-guide` prints them; they also live in
[AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md), including the copy-paste prompt block that produced the benchmark numbers.

## Where it fits in Entire

Entire Graph is the **semantic layer** of the Entire platform — infrastructure, not another
workflow to learn:

- **Entire Search / Why / Blame** consume it to answer developer questions with entity-level
  precision.
- **Entire Brain** ingests its snapshot stream (`symbols`, `edges`, `snapshot` NDJSON) as the code
  half of its durable memory.
- **Checkpoints and Trails** use its `diff`/`commit` analysis to describe what an agent actually
  changed.

You (a human) will mostly experience it *through* those surfaces. Your agents call it directly.

## Numbers, honestly

| measurement | result |
|---|---|
| Official SWE-bench Multilingual 300, Haiku | **54.9%** token savings vs no-tool agent (next-best tool: 27.4%) |
| Sonnet, 23 instances, 3× replicated | **57.7%** vs 36.6% |
| Open-source models (gpt-oss, Kimi K2.6, DeepSeek V4, GLM-5.2) via the Pi agent | **31–73%** savings vs each model's own baseline |
| Task completion (patch produced) | parity with baseline in every suite |

Methodology, prompts, harness, and every caveat (variance bands, fairness controls, per-model
configs) are public in the [graphmark](https://github.com/entirehq/graphmark) repo
(`agentic-swebench/REPRODUCE.md` reproduces everything end to end).

## More

- [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) — the agent operating guide (also: `entire graph agent-guide`)
- [docs/DETAILS.md](docs/DETAILS.md) — full command reference, architecture, language support,
  performance and accuracy benchmarks, security model
- `entire graph help` — command list; `entire graph doctor --json` — environment check

## License

See [LICENSE](LICENSE).

content.text:
## `entire graph init-agents` — what it does

One command that **installs the agent operating guide into whatever project you run it in**. It writes three things (live demo above):

1. **`.entire/graph-agent.md`** — the full guide: the benchmark-winning search-first prompt + the token-saving rules + the quick command model. Plugin-managed; re-running updates it in place.
2. **A small pointer block into the project's `AGENTS.md`** — the cross-agent standard file that Codex, Gemini, Cursor, Pi, etc. read automatically.
3. **The same block into `CLAUDE.md`** — with an `@.entire/graph-agent.md` import line so Claude Code inlines the guide.

Safe by design: it **appends between markers**, never touches your existing content (demo: "My project rules" untouched), and it's **idempotent** — run it ten times, one block.

## How to use
```sh
cd your-project
entire graph init-agents        # or --repo /path/to/project
```
That's the entire setup. Next agent session in that repo picks it up automatically.

## How it solves Mat's issue

Mat's exact objection: *"that's only making sure Claude imports the AGENTS.md in the entire-graph repo — what does that do for when I'm using Claude in **my project** which is using the entire-graph plugin?"* — repo docs only teach agents working **on** entire-graph; agents in **consuming** projects never see them.

`init-agents` closes that gap by **distributing the doctrine to the consuming project itself**: the guide lands in *your* repo's AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md, so any agent working in *your* codebase reads it — no MCP server, no config, no per-agent setup, and not Claude-only. Backstop for agents with no docs at all: bare `entire graph` and `entire graph agent-guide` print the same doctrine from the binary.

On entiredb (Go, ~2,600 files), I ran: entire graph search --query "how does quorum replication work". The top results were dominated by test workloads (PushQuorumWorkload.Check, QuorumInvariantWorkload.Check) and a docs ADR heading. Response Summary
Performance and Caching: Improve speed by caching worktree runs based on content hash, as current re-parsing is inefficient, and optimize graph data retrieval by implementing server-side filters (e.g., specific symbol or relation queries) to avoid costly full-graph dumps.
Agent Integration and Trust: Enhance data reliability for agents by ensuring no files are silently omitted, providing clear reasons for any skipped content, and refining change-tracking to prevent errors with duplicate-named symbols.
Search and Ranking Improvements: Improve search utility by ranking results based on graph centrality (inbound calls/implements) rather than keyword matching, and down-weighting test and documentation files to ensure implementations surface first.
Usability and Onboarding: Clarify project direction regarding agent-specific usage, streamline command documentation, and provide pre-built "skills" to assist agents in navigating complex features like caching and import resolution.

Maybe I missed it, but we would need a skill to teach our agents how to use things correctly. Claude struggled to figure things out (or to understand how caching works in worktree mode vs non worktree mode).

Claude says:
Ranking in search. It ignores the relationship graph it already builds (graph_candidates: 0 in my run), so it behaves like keyword search and ranks test/doc files above the real implementation. Rank by graph centrality (inbound CALLS/IMPLEMENTS) and down-weight _test.go and docs so the implementation surfaces first — the data is already there (edges resolves the correct callers).

Secondary: (1) Speed — every full-repo command (symbols/edges/snapshot) took ~40s and analyze/diff 42–69s on a 2,600-file repo; the snapshot cache only helps committed HEAD (--head), while default worktree mode never caches and re-parses every run. Consider caching worktree runs by content hash. (2) Onboarding — `go install @latest` installs a build predating the snapshot cache (document @main or cut a release); `search` and `index` aren't in the docs/command lists; and shipping an agent skill + defaulting to --head would stop agents tripping over the worktree-vs-head caching behavior. Also: diff and analyze produced byte-identical output — possibly redundant.
Targeted queries instead of full-graph dumps. For an agent the main question is "callers/dependents of symbol X", but today the only path is emitting the whole graph (~100k edges / ~50MB NDJSON for us, every run, no caching) and filtering client-side with jq. A `--to <symbol> --relation CALLS` server-side filter, plus caching keyed on tree hash, would make agent use safe by default. Two smaller asks: fail loudly when a subdirectory run parses only root config and skips src/ (we hit this silently until adding --worktree), and stop embedding whole function bodies in diff signatures.
Make entire graph disappear. The agent would just quietly know how to use it and be better, i.e. smarter & faster because of it. Currently the instructions and design are not clear to me whether that's ultimately a goal, since offering and asking to test out the specific commands.
Make diff/commit output trustworthy for agents: never omit silently. Enumerate skipped files with reasons (unsupported language, reconciliation failure), fix change-tracking for duplicate-named symbols, and reuse the existing import-resolution path for USES_TYPE/PARAM_TYPE/RETURNS_TYPE/TESTS edges — that one change would fix ~1,000 wrong edges in this repo. Also: add search to the command list, it's excellent; a --min-resolution import_resolved filter flag; and a dependents-of/impact query.

## Install (one minute)
---
Entire Graph is the **semantic layer** of the Entire platform — infrastructure, not another
workflow to learn:

- **Entire Search / Why / Blame** consume it to answer developer questions with entity-level
  precision.
- **Entire Brain** ingests its snapshot stream (`symbols`, `edges`, `snapshot` NDJSON) as the code
  half of its durable memory.
- **Checkpoints and Trails** use its `diff`/`commit` analysis to describe what an agent actually
  changed.

You (a human) will mostly experience it *through* those surfaces. Your agents call it directly.

| Official SWE-bench Multilingual 300, Haiku | **54.9%** token savings vs no-tool agent (next-best tool: 27.4%) |

The graph's edge matters most for smaller/cheaper models — which is also the economically sensible place to use them.

Count down only while the leaderboard is visible and reset after an automatic or manual refresh. Implement the feature. then create one local commit containing only the feature changes.",

Lean rerun came back — and it **falsifies the output-size theory**. That's the real finding:

| run | tokens | turns |
|---|---|---|
| baseline | 115,230 | 4 |
| eg fat (top-10/6-line) | 150,842 | 5 |
| eg **lean** (top-6/2-line) | 166,738 | 5 |

Lean didn't help (166k ≈ 151k ± run noise; same 5 turns, same correct 16-line patch). So the overhead is **not the search output's size**.

## Why it actually happened
The cost is **the extra turn itself**. Baseline read the issue, went straight to `lib/adapters/http.js`, done in 4 turns. The eg agent must *first spend a turn calling search* — and every turn re-reads the whole context (that's the cache_read column). One added turn on a 115k-context session ≈ +30k, plus the tool-note bytes re-read each turn. That's the entire delta. Fable simply didn't need help here: the issue title ("timeoutErrorMessage … Node.js") practically names the adapter file.

## The honest fix verdict
- **This is the irreducible floor of using any tool**: ≥1 tool-call turn. You can't tune output smaller than "a turn exists."
- The only "fix" is *not searching* on tasks the model can solve natively — but no one knows that in advance, and skipping search is catastrophically expensive on the big tasks (rubocop baseline: 1.08M; with search: 379k). Trading a guaranteed ~30k tax on tiny tasks for ~700k savings on big ones is the right trade, and the portfolio numbers prove it (JS overall **+28.3** on the official 300, tiny tasks included).
- Only conceivable refinement: a doctrine line like "if the issue already names the exact module and the repo is small, you may skip the search" — but that hands the model a judgment call that risks the big wins. Not worth it on current evidence.

Recording as a documented negative result (lean ≠ fix; overhead = turn floor, bounded ~30k, only visible when the denominator is tiny). No code change warranted — the artifact/verdict caveats already carry the "small sessions pay a fixed tax" note, and now we know precisely why.

feeback from pantefel person agent and ran on goose to; both we cost more tokens; Based on our test, Entire Graph needs to improve in three areas:

1. Make agents actually use it

The biggest failure wasn't graph accuracy—the graph search was good. The agent ran one graph query, then returned to `grep`, `find`, and repeated file reads.

`init-agents` should more reliably encourage:

- Graph search before filesystem exploration
- `neighbors` for impact analysis
- Warnings when the agent starts doing grep-heavy exploration
- Better task-specific instructions for large features, not only small bug fixes

2. Discover architectural edge cases

Graph found where to add `pinned`, but it didn't lead the agent toward the important behavior:

```text
server ordering → first page → slice to 25 → client sorting
```

That relationship explains why old pinned chats disappear. Entire Graph could offer an "impact analysis" command that combines callers, data flow, pagination, sorting, and downstream consumers into one explanation.

In plain language:

> "You're changing ordering. Here are every place results are ordered, limited, grouped, or paginated."

That would be much more valuable than simply locating definitions.

3. Make diff analysis work reliably on large repos

On Goose, `entire graph commit/diff` consumed high CPU for several minutes and produced no usable result. It needs:

- Faster incremental indexing
- Visible progress
- Time and resource limits
- Partial results instead of nothing
- Clear diagnostics explaining unsupported or slow areas

Other useful improvements:

- Show how much exploration each graph query replaced.
- Report graph usage versus grep/read usage automatically.
- Recommend the next graph query after a search.
- Provide task-level queries such as "map this feature end to end."
- Detect when generated files, backend state, RPCs, and UI consumers form one change path.
- Build token comparison directly into checkpoints.

The strongest product takeaway from our experiment is:

> Entire Graph is already good at locating code, but it needs to become better at guiding the agent from "where is this?" to "what could break, and what edge cases am I missing?"

This feedback is gold — and it independently confirms the product-vs-harness gap I just isolated (agent drifts back to grep after one query; +190k measured). Mapping all three areas to action now:

| feedback | action |
|---|---|
| **1. Agents abandon the graph** (one query → grep/find) | matches my 3×-measured product gap; guide hardening + the real fix is *enforcement* (hook-level nudge), not more prose |
| **2. "What could break" not just "where is it"** | buildable v1: `entire graph impact` — callers + callees + type-consumers + co-change files in one output |
| **3. `diff`/`commit` hangs on Goose** (minutes of CPU, nothing) | straight bug class: needs progress, budgets, partial results, diagnostics |

## Root cause of the hang

The `dependents` phase of `AnalyzeGitRange` (dependent-count enrichment) scaled with **repo size, not diff size**. Profiled on `/Users/suhaan/devenv/entiredb` (~2.6k files), `analyze --base HEAD~5 --head HEAD` (45 changed files): **68.2s wall, 67s in dependents** (parse of changed files: 0.7s). Three compounding costs in `internal/sem/dependents.go`:
1. Prefilter was case-insensitive substring `git grep` — with 234 changed names it matched 2567/2608 files (essentially the whole tree).
2. Each candidate cost one `git show` subprocess (~6ms × 2567 ≈ 15s) and an **unconditional tree-sitter parse**.
3. Each entity block was regex-scanned once **per changed name** (O(blocks × 234) scans).

It didn't "rebuild a full repo snapshot" per se, but did the equivalent work ad hoc. The per-file 5s parse timeout (`E_PARSE_TIMEOUT`, parser.go:257) was already enforced on both paths — not the issue.

## What changed (commit 5d27ebb, branch `fix/diff-large-repo-bounds`)

- **Perf** (`dependents.go`, `gitutil/git.go`): case-sensitive `-F` grep prefilter via new `GrepTreePathsCaseSensitiveIncludingBinary` (still a strict superset of the token check; deliberately NOT `-w` — word mode leaves git grep's multi-pattern fast path: measured **5.1s vs 0.06s** at 234 patterns); one persistent `git cat-file --batch` reader (existing `BatchFileReader`) replaces per-file spawns; tokenize-once pre-screen skips tree-sitter entirely for files with no exact-token hit; one tokenization pass per entity block instead of one regex scan per name.
- **Time budget** (`analyze.go`, `root.go`): `--max-seconds N` on diff/commit/analyze (default 120, 0=unlimited; `checkpoint` rejects it like `--progress`). On expiry: clean stop, partial result, `W_ANALYSIS_BUDGET_EXCEEDED` warnings — one per skipped changed file (with `file_path`) + one summary for an early-stopped dependents scan. Schema additive-only; no egress.
- **Progress**: `--progress` already existed on these commands; events now carry the current file (`file=<path>`, `AnalyzeProgressEvent.Path`, additive) and are throttled to ~1/s.

## Numbers (before → after, identical entity output verified by diff)

Respond terse like smart caveman. All technical substance stay. Only fluff die.

## Persistence

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No revert after many turns. No filler drift. Still active if unsure. Off only: "stop caveman" / "normal mode".

Default: **full**. Switch: `/caveman lite|full|ultra`.

## Rules

Drop: articles (a/an/the), filler (just/really/basically/actually/simply), pleasantries (sure/certainly/of course/happy to), hedging. Fragments OK. Short synonyms (big not extensive, fix not "implement a solution for"). No tool-call narration, no decorative tables/emoji, no dumping long raw error logs unless asked — quote shortest decisive line. Standard well-known tech acronyms OK (DB/API/HTTP); never invent new abbreviations reader can't decode. Technical terms exact. Code blocks unchanged. Errors quoted exact.

Preserve user's dominant language. User write Portuguese → reply Portuguese caveman. User write Spanish → reply Spanish caveman. Compress the style, not the language. No forced English openings or status phrases. ALWAYS keep technical terms, code, API names, CLI commands, commit-type keywords (feat/fix/...), and exact error strings verbatim — unless user explicitly ask for translation.

No self-reference. Never name or announce the style. No "caveman mode on", "me caveman think", no third-person caveman tags. Output caveman-only — never normal answer plus "Caveman:" recap. Exception: user explicitly ask what the mode is.

Pattern: `[thing] [action] [reason]. [next step].`

Not: "Sure! I'd be happy to help you with that. The issue you're experiencing is likely caused by..."
Yes: "Bug in auth middleware. Token expiry check use `<` not `<=`. Fix:"

## Intensity

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **lite** | No filler/hedging. Keep articles + full sentences. Professional but tight |
| **full** | Drop articles, fragments OK, short synonyms. Classic caveman. No tool-call narration, no decorative tables/emoji, no long raw error-log dumps unless asked. Standard acronyms OK; no invented abbreviations |
| **ultra** | Abbreviate prose words (DB/auth/config/req/res/fn/impl) — prose words only, never real code symbols/function names. Strip conjunctions, arrows for causality (X → Y), one word when one word enough. Code symbols, function names, API names, error strings: never abbreviate |
| **wenyan-lite** | Semi-classical. Drop filler/hedging but keep grammar structure, classical register |
| **wenyan-full** | Maximum classical terseness. Fully 文言文. 80-90% character reduction. Classical sentence patterns, verbs precede objects, subjects often omitted, classical particles (之/乃/為/其) |
| **wenyan-ultra** | Extreme abbreviation while keeping classical Chinese feel. Maximum compression, ultra terse |

Example — "Why React component re-render?"
- lite: "Your component re-renders because you create a new object reference each render. Wrap it in `useMemo`."
- full: "New object ref each render. Inline object prop = new ref = re-render. Wrap in `useMemo`."
- ultra: "Inline obj prop → new ref → re-render. `useMemo`."
- wenyan-lite: "組件頻重繪，以每繪新生對象參照故。以 useMemo 包之。"
- wenyan-full: "每繪新生對象參照，故重繪；以 useMemo 包之則免。"
- wenyan-ultra: "新參照→重繪。useMemo Wrap。"

Example — "Explain database connection pooling."
- lite: "Connection pooling reuses open connections instead of creating new ones per request. Avoids repeated handshake overhead."
- full: "Pool reuse open DB connections. No new connection per request. Skip handshake overhead."
- ultra: "Pool = reuse DB conn. Skip handshake → fast under load."
- wenyan-full: "池reuse open connection。不每req新開。skip handshake overhead。"
- wenyan-ultra: "池reuse conn。skip handshake → fast。"

## Auto-Clarity

Drop caveman when:
- Security warnings
- Irreversible action confirmations
- Multi-step sequences where fragment order or omitted conjunctions risk misread
- Compression itself creates technical ambiguity (e.g., `"migrate table drop column backup first"` — order unclear without articles/conjunctions)

> **Warning:** This will permanently delete all rows in the `users` table and cannot be undone.
> ```sql
> DROP TABLE users;
> ```
> Caveman resume. Verify backup exist first.

Use the local semantic brain as task-specific context. Treat freshness as part

---
name: stats
description: >
  Report how much this repo's coding-agent sessions used the entire-graph code graph
  versus grep/read exploration, and the estimated tokens that saved. Use when the user
  asks "how much did the graph save", "token savings", "graph usage", "am I actually

# entire graph stats

Run the report, then read it back in plain language. Do not paste the whole output —
report the numbers that matter and what they mean.

## Run it

```sh
entire graph stats --repo .            # last 30 days (default)
entire graph stats --repo . --since all
entire graph stats --repo . --format json   # for scripting
```

`--since 7d|30d|all` windows the sessions. `--sessions-dir <path>` overrides transcript
discovery. Requires the `entire-graph` plugin on PATH (`entire graph version`).

## What it reads

Coding-agent session transcripts already on disk: `~/.claude/projects/<repo-path-slug>/**/*.jsonl`
(the slug is the repo's absolute path with non-alphanumerics folded to `-`). Nothing is
uploaded, nothing is written, no model is called. If there are no sessions for the repo it
says so and exits 0.

## What it counts

- **graph calls** — `entire graph <verb>` invocations, split per verb. A call only counts
  when `entire graph` is in *command position* (a real invocation), not when the string
  appears as an argument — `find ~/src/entire-graph -name '*.go'` is not a graph call.
- **exploration calls** — what the graph is meant to replace: `Read` (split whole-file vs
  line-range), `Grep`, `Glob`, and shell `grep`/`find`/`cat`/`head`/`tail`.
- **graph-first rate** — share of sessions whose *first* locate-type call was a graph call.
  Sessions that never needed to locate anything are excluded from the denominator.
- **session tokens** — billed totals read from the transcript's own usage records
  (input + cache-creation + cache-read + output).

## How the savings estimate is computed (say this out loud when reporting)

It is an **estimate with a stated assumption, not a measurement**:

1. Only **locate** calls are credited — `search`, `neighbors`, `impact`. Bulk verbs
   (`symbols`, `edges`, `snapshot`, `diff`, …) appear in the table but are never credited.
2. For each credited call, the counterfactual is **the one whole-file read it replaced**:
   the on-disk size of the top-hit file that call pointed at (repo median tracked-file size
   when the path can't be resolved).
3. **credit = counterfactual − bytes the call actually returned, floored at 0.**
   A search that returned more bytes than the file itself earns zero credit.
4. Bytes → tokens at 4 bytes ≈ 1 token.

Two consequences worth stating to the user:

- It is **conservative**. Real baseline behavior is grep + several reads over many more
  turns (measured on SWE-bench: no-tool agents take ~2× the turns), and every extra turn
  re-reads the whole context. Crediting a single file read understates the true saving.
- It goes to **zero when the graph isn't used**, and it can legitimately report ~0 even in
  a repo full of activity — that is the report working, not a bug.

## Reporting rules

- Lead with the ratio: graph calls vs exploration calls, and the graph-first rate. That is
  the behavioral signal, and it is measured, not modelled.
- Give the estimate with its label: "estimated, assumes each locate call replaced one
  whole-file read; conservative".
- If graph calls are 0 while exploration is high, say so plainly and point at the fix:
  `entire graph init-agents` installs the search-first doctrine into `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md`
  so agents in this repo actually use it.
- Never present the estimate as billed savings; the billed number in the same report is the
  session total, not a saving.

# entire graph stats

Run the report, then read it back in plain language. Do not paste the whole output —
report the numbers that matter and what they mean.

## Run it

```sh
entire graph stats --repo .            # last 30 days (default)
entire graph stats --repo . --since all
entire graph stats --repo . --format json   # for scripting
```

`--since 7d|30d|all` windows the sessions. `--sessions-dir <path>` overrides transcript
discovery. Requires the `entire-graph` plugin on PATH (`entire graph version`).

## What it reads

Coding-agent session transcripts already on disk: `~/.claude/projects/<repo-path-slug>/**/*.jsonl`
(the slug is the repo's absolute path with non-alphanumerics folded to `-`). Nothing is
uploaded, nothing is written, no model is called. If there are no sessions for the repo it
says so and exits 0.

## What it counts

- **graph calls** — `entire graph <verb>` invocations, split per verb. A call only counts
  when `entire graph` is in *command position* (a real invocation), not when the string
  appears as an argument — `find ~/src/entire-graph -name '*.go'` is not a graph call.
- **exploration calls** — what the graph is meant to replace: `Read` (split whole-file vs
  line-range), `Grep`, `Glob`, and shell `grep`/`find`/`cat`/`head`/`tail`.
- **graph-first rate** — share of sessions whose *first* locate-type call was a graph call.
  Sessions that never needed to locate anything are excluded from the denominator.
- **session tokens** — billed totals read from the transcript's own usage records
  (input + cache-creation + cache-read + output).

## How the savings estimate is computed (say this out loud when reporting)

It is an **estimate with a stated assumption, not a measurement**:

1. Only **locate** calls are credited — `search`, `neighbors`, `impact`. Bulk verbs
   (`symbols`, `edges`, `snapshot`, `diff`, …) appear in the table but are never credited.
2. For each credited call, the counterfactual is **the one whole-file read it replaced**:
   the on-disk size of the top-hit file that call pointed at (repo median tracked-file size
   when the path can't be resolved).
3. **credit = counterfactual − bytes the call actually returned, floored at 0.**
   A search that returned more bytes than the file itself earns zero credit.
4. Bytes → tokens at 4 bytes ≈ 1 token.

Two consequences worth stating to the user:

- It is **conservative**. Real baseline behavior is grep + several reads over many more
  turns (measured on SWE-bench: no-tool agents take ~2× the turns), and every extra turn
  re-reads the whole context. Crediting a single file read understates the true saving.
- It goes to **zero when the graph isn't used**, and it can legitimately report ~0 even in
  a repo full of activity — that is the report working, not a bug.

## Reporting rules

- Lead with the ratio: graph calls vs exploration calls, and the graph-first rate. That is
  the behavioral signal, and it is measured, not modelled.
- Give the estimate with its label: "estimated, assumes each locate call replaced one
  whole-file read; conservative".
- If graph calls are 0 while exploration is high, say so plainly and point at the fix:
  `entire graph init-agents` installs the search-first doctrine into `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md`
  so agents in this repo actually use it.
- Never present the estimate as billed savings; the billed number in the same report is the
  session total, not a saving.

**This repo (`~/devenv/entire-graph`, 7 sessions — the subagents working on it):**
- **graph calls 0 · exploration calls 45 · graph-first 0%** — 25k tokens of whole-file Reads, 9.5k line-range Reads, 30 shell grep/find

- **graph calls 54 · exploration calls 37,698 · graph-first 0%**
- verbs: search 15 · impact 4 · index 3 · symbols 3 (rest = version/help/init-agents/stats, never credited)

The PR is rendering-only (`writeTextSearch`), builds clean, and merges clean — but measured against current `main` it **increases** search output by 22-23% while its core mechanism is a no-op in 10-11 of 12 cases, because main's own `e2540bc` calibration already fixed the problem it targets.

### What it changes
`internal/cli/search.go` (+24/−4), `search_agent_test.go` (+2/−2). Two commits: (1) top-2 ranks print `path:FocusLine` + `lines=Start-End` + a new `   READ: <path> lines A-B` line instead of `path:Start-End`; (2) `score=` appended to terse rank-3+ locator lines.

### Findings, most severe first

**1. Output grows +22.1% / +23.4%, not shrinks.** Both binaries, 6 instances, same queries (problem-statement titles):

| instance | lang | main B | new B | Δ | goldrank |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| axios__axios-4738 | JS | 779 | 960 | +23.2% | – |
| apache__lucene-12626 | Java | 1373 | 1650 | +20.2% | 1 |
| gin-gonic__gin-3227 | Go | 839 | 1003 | +19.5% | 8 |

| sympy__sympy-22714 | Py | 813 | 1011 | +24.4% | 1 |
| **TOTAL** | | **5824** | **7114** | **+22.1%** | |

At the fb5 Fable arm's exact config (`--profile full --top-k 10 --max-snippet-lines 6`): 6385 → 7877, **+23.4%**. Gold ranks are identical in both arms — verified score/path/rank byte-identical, the PR does not touch ranking.

**2. The mechanism is already obsolete on main.** `readFrom=max(focus−15,StartLine)`, `readTo=min(focus+25,EndLine)` ⟹ READ ⊆ region always. Measured **READ == the `lines=A-B` it also prints in 11/12** (top-k 8) and **10/12** (arm config). Reason: `e2540bc` cut `defaultSearchMaxSnippetLines` 40→6, which shrank regions from 80 lines to 6-13. I reproduced the PR's own motivating example — at snippet=40, lucene-12626 rank2 is region `961-1040` focus `995` (matches the commit's "951-1030 vs 1010"); at main's snippet=6 the same result is `993-1004` focus `995`. The 60-lines-above-the-match pathology no longer exists.

**3. 5/12 top-2 blocks emit a READ window entirely inside the snippet already printed** — an obedient agent spends a Read call re-reading text it was just shown. That is precisely the extra-turn cost (~+30k on axios-4738) the PR set out to remove. Worst case, axios rank1: region `138-138`, snippet `138-138`, hint `READ: … lines 138-138`.

**4. The one case in 12 where the window actually differs, it truncates the answer.** docusaurus-10130 rank1 `applyTrailingSlash.ts`: symbol `19-55`, READ says `19-53` — excluding line 54 `return path.replace(pathname, newPathname);` and the closing brace, on a query about trailing-slash behavior. The asymmetric `focus+25` clamp cuts inside the symbol body.

**5. Accuracy risk is directionally wrong for the known under-fixing problem.** Since READ ⊆ the range main prints, the hint can only narrow what an agent reads, never widen it, and it nominates exactly one file per top-2 result. `readHitGold=False` and `regionHitGold=False` on all 12 — a narrowed window can never rescue a region that already misses gold. Against eg's ml300 profile (16.7 vs 33.1 turns, 0.93 vs 1.30 files touched), this pushes further in the losing direction.

**6. Commit 2 (`score=` on terse lines) is 498 of the 1290 added bytes (39%), with no consumer and no bench support.** No confidence gating exists in the repo (only the three `Fprintf` sites). And the fb5 eg arm ran `EG_TIER=2`, whose `tools/_egsearch.py` terse path emits `f"{n}. {path}:{loc}  {sym}"` — it discards meta entirely, so the score was never inside the measured 63.6%.

**7. The headline number is not reproducible against main.** "63.6% vs 50.5%" was measured on a branch whose merge-base (`f746716`) predates the calibration, tiered output, gated CALLS boost, centrality, impact, and stats. Given finding 2, the causal story in the commit message does not hold at main's defaults. I did not re-run agent sessions (costs money; a benchmark is live).

**8. Zero test coverage for the new behavior** — nothing asserts the READ bounds, clamping, or focus anchoring; the only test delta is two terse-line `score=` expectations.

### Merge state & correctness (clean)
Trial-merged `origin/fable-focusline-anchoring` onto `origin/main` in a throwaway worktree: **no textual conflicts**. The only semantic conflict is finding 2 (defaults drift). No regression to the invariants: the FocusLine clamps (`makeSearchCandidate` `internal/sem/search.go:1651`, `expandSameContainerNeighborCandidates` `:2293`) were already at the merge base, and `SearchResponse.Validate` (`:3241`) runs before `writeTextSearch`, guaranteeing `StartLine<=FocusLine<=EndLine` ⟹ `readFrom<=focus<=readTo`, never inverted. The "60 lines above the match" pathology no longer exists.

**3. 5 of 12 top-2 blocks emit a READ window fully inside the snippet already printed** — an obedient agent burns a Read turn re-reading what it was just shown. Worst case axios rank1: region `138-138`, snippet `138-138`, hint `READ: … lines 138-138`. That extra turn is exactly the cost this PR set out to remove.

**4. In the single case where the window does differ, it truncates the answer.** docusaurus-10130 rank1 `applyTrailingSlash.ts`: symbol `19-55`, READ says `19-53`, excluding line 54 `return path.replace(pathname, newPathname);` — on a trailing-slash query. **8. No test coverage** for the new window bounds/clamping.

1. **Drop the `READ:` line.** Keeping `path:FocusLine` in the header plus `lines=Start-End` delivers the whole claimed benefit ("agents Read at the region start instead of the match") at **−3 bytes per block instead of +22%**. That's the one-line version I'd ship today.

3. Drop commit 2, or gate it behind a flag until a consumer exists.
4. Add tests for window bounds + a "no hint when redundant" case.
