#!/bin/sh
# entire-graph — status line badge for Claude Code.
#
# Renders one line summarising what the code graph bought you in THIS session:
#
#   [GRAPH] ↗ 2.1M saved · 34 search · 7 impact · graph-first ✓ · 61% of locates · 12% of session
#
# Claude Code invokes a status line command with the session JSON on stdin and takes stdout as
# the badge (ANSI colour is allowed). The fields consumed here:
#
#   .transcript_path        path to this session's JSONL transcript  (required)
#   .workspace.current_dir  repo to resolve the savings counterfactual against
#   .cwd                    fallback for the above
#   .session_id             cache key
#
# Every number comes from `entire graph stats --transcript <path> --format json`, so the
# accounting is exactly internal/cli/stats.go — command-position-only graph verbs against a
# closed verb allowlist, locate verbs (search/neighbors/impact) alone credited, credit =
# top-hit-file size − returned bytes floored at 0, 4 bytes = 1 token. There is no second
# estimator here to drift out of sync.
#
# Enable it in ~/.claude/settings.json:
#   "statusLine": { "type": "command",
#                   "command": "sh /path/to/scripts/entire-graph-statusline.sh" }
#
# Environment:
#   ENTIRE_GRAPH_BIN               explicit path to the entire-graph binary
#   ENTIRE_GRAPH_STATUSLINE_SCOPE  session (default) | project
#                                  project re-scans the whole ~/.claude/projects/<slug>
#                                  directory — hundreds of MB on a busy project, and far too
#                                  slow to render per keystroke. Opt in knowingly.
#   ENTIRE_GRAPH_STATUSLINE_SINCE  window for scope=project (default 30d)
#   ENTIRE_GRAPH_STATUSLINE_CACHE  0 disables the render cache (always recompute, in-line)
#   NO_COLOR                       set to any value to drop ANSI escapes
#
# Prints NOTHING and exits 0 on every failure: no binary, no transcript, unparseable JSON,
# no sessions. A status line must never surface an error or hang.

set -u

# Never let a stray diagnostic from a child process reach the status line.
exec 2>/dev/null

SCOPE=${ENTIRE_GRAPH_STATUSLINE_SCOPE:-session}
SINCE=${ENTIRE_GRAPH_STATUSLINE_SINCE:-30d}

# --- stdin ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# One awk pass pulls the three fields out of the session JSON. Always three lines, "-" for a
# field that is absent, so word splitting downstream can never shift the fields.
META=$(
	awk '
		function field(key,   pat, raw) {
			pat = "\"" key "\"[ \t]*:[ \t]*\"[^\"]*\""
			if (!match(blob, pat)) return "-"
			raw = substr(blob, RSTART, RLENGTH)
			sub(/^[^:]*:[ \t]*"/, "", raw)
			sub(/"$/, "", raw)
			if (raw == "") return "-"
			return raw
		}
		{ blob = blob $0 }
		END {
			dir = field("current_dir")
			if (dir == "-") dir = field("cwd")
			print field("transcript_path")
			print dir
			print field("session_id")
		}
	'
) || exit 0

IFS='
'
# shellcheck disable=SC2086 # deliberate: split META on newlines only
set -- $META
unset IFS
[ "$#" -eq 3 ] || exit 0
TRANSCRIPT=$1
REPO=$2
SESSION=$3

[ "$TRANSCRIPT" = "-" ] && exit 0
[ -f "$TRANSCRIPT" ] || exit 0
[ -s "$TRANSCRIPT" ] || exit 0
[ "$REPO" = "-" ] && REPO=$PWD
[ -d "$REPO" ] || REPO=$PWD

# --- binary --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
BIN=
for candidate in \
	"${ENTIRE_GRAPH_BIN:-}" \
	"${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT:-}${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT:+/entire-graph}" \
	"${GOBIN:-}${GOBIN:+/entire-graph}" \
	"${HOME}/go/bin/entire-graph"; do
	if [ -n "$candidate" ] && [ -x "$candidate" ]; then
		BIN=$candidate
		break
	fi
done
if [ -z "$BIN" ]; then
	BIN=$(command -v entire-graph) || BIN=
fi
[ -n "$BIN" ] || exit 0

# --- measure + render ----------------------------------------------------------------------
render() {
	if [ "$SCOPE" = "project" ]; then
		report=$("$BIN" stats --repo "$REPO" --sessions-dir "$(dirname "$TRANSCRIPT")" \
			--since "$SINCE" --format json 2>/dev/null) || return 1
	else
		report=$("$BIN" stats --repo "$REPO" --transcript "$TRANSCRIPT" \
			--since all --format json 2>/dev/null) || return 1
	fi
	case $report in
	'{'*) ;;
	*) return 1 ;;
	esac

	color=1
	[ -n "${NO_COLOR:-}" ] && color=0

	printf '%s' "$report" | awk -v color="$color" '
		function number(key,   pat, raw) {
			pat = "\"" key "\"[ \t]*:[ \t]*-?[0-9][0-9.eE+-]*"
			if (!match(blob, pat)) return -1
			raw = substr(blob, RSTART, RLENGTH)
			sub(/^[^:]*:[ \t]*/, "", raw)
			return raw + 0
		}
		# 532 -> "532", 12345 -> "12.3K", 2000000 -> "2M", 2100000 -> "2.1M".
		# NB: no backreference in the sub() — POSIX awk only understands "&", so the unit is
		# appended after trimming rather than captured.
		function human(value,   text, unit) {
			if (value < 1000) return sprintf("%d", value)
			if (value < 1000000) { text = sprintf("%.1f", value / 1000); unit = "K" }
			else { text = sprintf("%.1f", value / 1000000); unit = "M" }
			sub(/\.0$/, "", text)
			return text unit
		}
		function pct(value) {
			if (value >= 10) return sprintf("%d%%", value + 0.5)
			if (value >= 1) return sprintf("%.1f%%", value)
			return sprintf("%.2f%%", value)
		}
		function paint(text, code) {
			if (!color) return text
			return "\033[" code "m" text "\033[0m"
		}
		function sep() { return paint(" \302\267 ", "2") }
		# Verb names are rendered into the terminal, so keep them to the closed lowercase set
		# the CLI dispatches and cap the length: a status line must never echo arbitrary bytes.
		function clean(name) {
			gsub(/[^a-z-]/, "", name)
			return substr(name, 1, 16)
		}
		{ blob = blob $0 }
		END {
			sessions = number("sessions")
			graph    = number("graph_calls")
			explore  = number("exploration_calls")
			if (sessions <= 0) exit 0

			label = paint("[GRAPH]", "38;5;45")

			if (graph <= 0) {
				out = label " " paint("no graph calls yet", "2")
				if (explore > 0) out = out sep() paint(explore " explore", "2")
				print out
				exit 0
			}

			saved    = number("estimated_savings_est_tokens")
			savedPct = number("estimated_savings_pct_of_session_tokens")
			gfHit    = number("graph_first_sessions")
			gfTotal  = number("sessions_with_locate")

			out = label " " paint("\342\206\227 " human(saved) " saved", "38;5;78")

			# Verb split. graph_calls_by_verb is already ordered calls-desc by the CLI.
			if (match(blob, /"graph_calls_by_verb"[ \t]*:[ \t]*\[[^]]*\]/)) {
				verbs = substr(blob, RSTART, RLENGTH)
				shown = 0
				counted = 0
				while (shown < 3 && match(verbs, /"name"[ \t]*:[ \t]*"[a-z-]+"[ \t]*,[ \t]*"calls"[ \t]*:[ \t]*[0-9]+/)) {
					entry = substr(verbs, RSTART, RLENGTH)
					verbs = substr(verbs, RSTART + RLENGTH)
					name = entry
					sub(/^"name"[ \t]*:[ \t]*"/, "", name)
					sub(/".*$/, "", name)
					calls = entry
					sub(/^.*"calls"[ \t]*:[ \t]*/, "", calls)
					calls = calls + 0
					name = clean(name)
					if (name == "" || calls <= 0) continue
					if (name == "neighbors") name = "nbrs"
					out = out sep() calls " " name
					counted += calls
					shown++
				}
				if (counted > 0 && counted < graph) out = out sep() (graph - counted) " other"

def load(run,arm):
    out={}
    for f in glob.glob(f'{AS}/results/{run}/{arm}/*/cc_out.json'):
        inst=f.split('/')[-2]
        try: j=json.load(open(f))

        u=j.get('usage',{})
        tok=sum(u.get(k,0) for k in ('input_tokens','cache_creation_input_tokens','cache_read_input_tokens','output_tokens'))
        p=f.replace('cc_out.json','patch.diff')
        lines=sum(1 for l in open(p) if l[:1] in '+-' and not l.startswith(('+++','---'))) if os.path.exists(p) else 0
        files=len({l.split()[-1] for l in open(p) if l.startswith('+++')}) if os.path.exists(p) else 0
        out[inst]=dict(tok=tok,turns=j.get('num_turns'),cost=j.get('total_cost_usd'),lines=lines,files=files)
    return out
runs=sorted({d.split('/')[-1] for d in glob.glob(f'{AS}/results/val30*')})

content.text:
Two findings worth stating plainly:

**1. The lever is turns, not bytes.** In v3, 95.9% of billed tokens are context re-read; a mean turn re-reads 47.5k tokens to return ~390 tokens of new information. One measured case: 7 consecutive `find`/`ls` turns returned 2,279 bytes and billed 579,549 tokens — 254 tokens per byte. So v6 doesn't forbid the work, it batches the turns: one Bash call instead of N, `git diff` once instead of re-reading edited files, test suite capped at twice (6 of 9 max-turns blowups were edit→run→edit loops chasing a green suite that never goes green). Modelled saving on the v3 transcripts: **−44%, 1.78M → ~0.99M**, with zero edit turns removed.

**2. `entire graph stats` has a real bug** — it sums usage per assistant *record*, but Claude Code writes several records per `message.id`, so session tokens are inflated ~2.3×. That number feeds the "% of session" segment on the status line I just shipped you. Fix is being made with before/after against ground truth from the benchmark's own `cc_out.json`.

entire-loop runs a bounded self-prompting agent-org "graph loop": a goal is
planned into worker seats (research, build, critic, measure) that fan out
concurrently with hybrid per-seat brain wiring, propose non-mutating changes,
and are verified and synthesized into a round result. Rounds repeat until the
goal is met or the round budget is spent.

Workers run in plan mode and never edit the target repo — they read, analyze,
and PROPOSE.

Usage:

  entire-loop [command]

Available Commands:

  help        Help about any command

  version     Print the plugin version

Run one bounded loop: plan → fan-out worker seats → verify → synthesize.
The goal is the remaining positional arguments joined together, so both
`entire loop run "fix the flaky test"` and `entire loop "fix the flaky test"` work.

Usage:
  entire-loop run <goal> [flags]

Flags:
      --allow-mutating-build     Let the build seat run a bypassPermissions coding agent in an isolated throwaway clone (default: plan-mode propose-as-text only)
      --converge-at float        Threshold value for --converge-metric (comparison is >= unless the inline "name<=value" form is used). Ignored when --converge-metric is unset
      --converge-metric string   Metric-threshold convergence (off by default). The metric name to watch, or an inline form "name>=value" / "name<=value". When set (with --converge-at, or the inline value), a round meets the goal — stopping the loop — once that metric crosses the threshold. This is the only way an external measurement stops the loop; usually paired with --measure-cmd
      --effort string            Worker reasoning effort, e.g. low, medium, high
  -h, --help                     help for run
      --jobs int                 Max concurrent worker seats (the CONC cap) (default 2)
      --max-rounds int           Safety cap on rounds in converge mode (default 6)
      --measure-cmd string       External measure command (off by default). Runs each round under a timeout (own process group, killed on timeout; stdout capped; env scrubbed); its JSON stdout (e.g. {"progress":0.8}) is parsed into typed round metrics that OVERRIDE the claude-derived ones and feed the reorg edge. It measures the mutating-build clone when one ran, else the repo root. By itself it does NOT stop the loop — pair it with --converge-metric to make a metric threshold end the run. Must be read-only (non-mutating) — the loop never grants it write privilege
      --model string             Worker model override (passed to claude --model)
      --plan-mode string         Plan-mutability axis (orthogonal to --planner): "dynamic" (re-plan the seat DAG every round from state — the graph rewrites itself) or "immutable" (plan the whole DAG ONCE up front, disable runtime reorg, and execute it every round with bounded per-node recovery — the fixed-script position) (default "dynamic")
      --planner string           Round planner: "llm" (self-planning control plane — an LLM control seat plans and re-plans each round; adds one control-seat cost per round) or "fixed" (static research/build/critic/measure roster) (default "llm")

Build a read-only measurement probe that an optimization loop (`entire loop run --measure-cmd`) will use to drive improvements to the entire-graph code-search tool. It must be DISCRIMINATIVE: unmodified main must score well below 1.0 so improvement is visible, and it must be impossible to score well without genuinely improving search output.

Context — what we measured and why this probe targets what it does:
- The accuracy gap between a graph-assisted agent and a no-tool baseline on SWE-bench Multilingual is NOT a ranking problem. The graph puts a gold file in the top 3 for 72.5% of lost instances and 81% of won ones, and the agent edits a gold file 82.7% of the time vs the baseline's 82.0% — locate is at parity.
- The cost is turns: 95.9% of billed tokens are context re-read, a mean turn re-reads ~47.5k tokens to return ~390 tokens of new information.
- So the tool-side lever is: ONE search call should return enough to make the fix correctly, so the agent needs fewer follow-up turns. Concretely — the gold symbol ranked in the top 3, the COMPLETE enclosing function body of the fix site (not a truncated window), and any sibling site with the same pattern — all within a tight byte budget.

Paths:
- graph tool source: /Users/suhaan/devenv/entire-graph (build: `go build -o /tmp/eg-probe ./cmd/entire-graph`; do NOT modify this repo, build only)
- benchmark suite: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-suhaan-devenv/7e3deab1-a028-46d5-9bf1-3318de93a0b6/scratchpad/graphmark/agentic-swebench (call it $AS)
- per-instance prebuilt graph dumps: $AS/graphs/<iid>/, wrapper $AS/tools/eg-q, existing probe to learn the conventions from: $AS/tools/measure_probe.sh
- gold patches + problem statements: $AS/tasks/pilot_tasks.json
- a prior agent's replay tooling lives in $AS/analysis/ — reuse it rather than rewriting if it fits.

Build $AS/tools/graph_quality_probe.sh that:
1. Uses a FIXED set of 10-14 instances spanning several languages, chosen from instances that have prebuilt graph dumps. Hard-code the list so the score is comparable across rounds. State which ones and why.
2. For each, runs ONE search with the query derived from the issue's first sentence (deterministic derivation, no cherry-picking per instance), and computes:
   - gold_top3: gold file (non-test file from the gold patch) ranked in top 3
   - gold_any: gold file present anywhere in results
   - encl_cov: does the returned snippet contain the COMPLETE enclosing function of the gold-patch hunk line (parse the function bounds from the graph's own symbol records; a snippet that stops short does not count)
   - sib_cov: when the gold patch touches >1 non-test site, does the result surface the second site too
   - bytes: bytes the call returned
3. Emits ONE line of JSON with the per-metric aggregates plus a `progress` score in [0,1] where guards are a GATE (multiply, not weight) and the frontier metrics carry the score, e.g. progress = guards_ok * (0.40*gold_top3_rate + 0.30*encl_cov_rate + 0.15*sib_cov_rate + 0.15*byte_score) with byte_score decreasing above a stated budget. Print the raw counts too, so a human can audit any score.
4. Is strictly READ-ONLY and non-mutating, finishes in a few minutes, uses only the prebuilt dumps + a built binary (no network, no docker), and takes the binary path from an env var (default /tmp/eg-probe) so the loop can point it at a modified clone.

- prove it is not a no-op: show at least two synthetic perturbations (e.g. force top-k to 1; truncate snippets to 2 lines) that move the score DOWN, with numbers.
- state clearly any metric you could not implement faithfully rather than approximating it silently.

Data-loss incident, contained. Reporting it straight because it cost real money:

**What happened.** `/private/tmp`'s mtime-based reaper deleted 1,622 tracked files from the graphmark checkout mid-run — including `collect_patch.sh`, the script that harvests each session's diff. Sessions kept running and paying, but `patch.diff` was never written and the worktrees were force-removed afterwards, so those results are unrecoverable.

**Cost:** ~94 sessions (~$23) produced nothing — both baseline repeats (30+30), 20 of v9, and 14 of the v3 repeat. That eval agent caught it and flagged that the still-running repeats were burning money for nothing; I killed the drivers and sessions immediately.

**Recovery:** all 1,622 files restored from git (everything I'd committed survived — the earlier decision to commit harness edits instead of leaving them loose is what saved this). Patch collection smoke-tested end to end before spending again: 454B diff written correctly. A keepalive now touches the suite tree every 10 min so the reaper can't eat it again.

**Relaunched:** baseline ×2 and v3 ×2 on the same 30, 6 sessions in flight. I'm not refilling v9 — v8 already showed the budget line trades accuracy away, so those 21 sessions aren't worth $6.

The graph-quality probe for the entire-loop run is still being built in parallel; that's unaffected, it lives in a different path.

content.text:
**On the fairness question — you were right to ask, and the answer is no, they weren't the same.**

The eg v3 arm's prompt carries a "(3) FIX IT PROPERLY" block (handle edge cases, change every site, re-read before finishing) that the baseline prompt never had. The baseline only ever got "Implement a correct, minimal, general fix." So v3's +3 instances is **confounded** — it could be the graph, or it could be that one instruction. I'd have been reporting a tool win that might just be a prompt win.

Two controls now in the harness, both committed:
- **`BASE_VERIFY`** — baseline gets the identical correctness wording, minus only the tool-specific lines a no-tool agent can't follow ("search first" needs a search tool). Running now, 2 rounds.
- **cmm verify parity** — cmm gets the *identical* v3 wording, only the command name differs, so eg-vs-cmm stays apples-to-apples.

For the record, the earlier arms were fair in the other direction: v1/v4/v5/cmm all shared identical search-only wording, and the baseline-vs-eg *token* comparisons are unaffected (the baseline has no tool note by construction — that's the point of a no-tool baseline). It's specifically the v3 **accuracy** claim that needed this control.

**Progress:** baseline plain r1 done (30/30), v3 repeat r1 at 29/30, controlled baseline just started, r2 rounds queued behind them. Graph loop still executing its rounds.

So the verdict table will now have four arms — baseline plain, baseline+fix-properly, eg v1, eg v3 — and only the eg-v3 vs baseline+fix-properly gap is honestly attributable to the graph.

content.text:
**30 instances out of the official 300**, unbiased sample, 23 repos across 9 languages (Java, Go, Rust, C, C++, PHP, Ruby, JS/TS). Model is Haiku throughout, exactly as you specified.

Why 30 and not 300: you said run smaller versions first for time efficiency. One 300-instance arm is ~10× the wall-clock and cost of a 30 — and I've now burned through 9 prompt variants, which at 300 each would have been unaffordable. The full-300 numbers already exist as the reference point from the earlier runs: **baseline 150/300 (50.0%), shipped eg 131/300 (43.7%)** — that's the gap that started this whole investigation.

Current inventory on the 30:

| run | rounds | status |
|---|---|---|
| baseline plain | r1 done, r2 running | 30/30 patches r1 |
| baseline + fix-properly (fairness control) | r1 running | just started |
| eg v3 | r1 (30/30, scored 21/28), + 2 repeats running | 29/30 on repeat r1 |
| v1/v4/v5/v6/v7/v8 | 1 each, all scored | done |

Once the repeats land, the honest comparison is 3× means of baseline vs 3× means of eg-v3 on the same 30, with the fix-properly control telling us how much of v3's gain is the graph versus the instruction. If eg-v3 clears the controlled baseline on those means, that's the 30/300 result — and the natural follow-up is to confirm it on the full 300, which is a single overnight run per arm rather than another round of variant search.

You're right that the comparison is rigged — just not in the direction it looks. Let me name the actual confound, because it's the whole ballgame.

The "search-first" note bundles **two different things**:
1. **tool-specific** — "search with `<tool>`", "don't grep to re-locate what search found"
2. **tool-agnostic frugality** — "reach the edit in as few turns as possible", "never read a whole file", "minimal fix, STOP the moment you can justify it"

Component 2 is a token lever that has *nothing to do with any tool* — any agent can be told to be frugal. In the original design, only the tool arms got it and the baseline never did. That's where a large chunk of the "+48% savings" came from. When I gave every arm the thorough wording, I removed component 2 from *everyone*, and the savings vanished. Both runs measured a prompt, not a tool.

So neither of my two configurations answers "does the tool save tokens". You need the factorial.

## The plan: 2×3 factorial, prompt family × tooling

| | baseline (no tool) | cmm | eg (us) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **frugal** (main's shipped doctrine) | to run | have (haiku), to run | have (haiku), to run |
| **thorough** (fix-properly) | ✅ done | ✅ done | ✅ done |

**Parity rule, enforced mechanically:** every arm gets component 2 verbatim; only component 1's locate line differs (`search with <tool>` vs `locate with grep/find`). I already prove this with a normalized diff that strips the tool path — eg vs cmm came out byte-identical last run.

**What each comparison then buys:**
- **eg vs baseline, same prompt column** → the tool's true contribution, frugality controlled for. This is the honest product claim.
- **frugal vs thorough column** → what the prompt alone is worth (the thing I've been accidentally measuring).
- **eg vs cmm, same cell** → the competitive head-to-head, uncontaminated. Your point about cmm stands here: it should look far better under a frugal prompt that actually tells the agent to use its memory instead of grepping.
- **tokens per *resolved* instance** → the number that matters commercially, since raw tokens are meaningless if accuracy moves.

Three tracks running toward the goal. Here's the plan and where it stands.

## Why the last result was wrong, precisely

Not because tools don't save — because **both my configurations compared a prompt, not a tool**. The tool note bundles tool-agnostic frugality ("as few turns as possible", "never read a whole file") with tool-specific usage. Give it only to tool arms → tools look great. Give the thorough note to everyone → tools look bad. Neither isolates the tool.

And separately: **our cmm wrapper was crippling cmm.** Its binary documents three combinable search modes (BM25 `query`, regex `name_pattern`, and `semantic_query` vector search that "finds 'publish' when you search 'send'"), plus `trace_path`, architecture overview, and pagination. `cmm-q` exposed BM25 and hand-rolled Cypher. Your instinct was right — cmm was being measured with one hand tied.

## The fix, in flight

**1. Fair per-tool doctrine** — restructuring prompts into two independent blocks: a SHARED block byte-identical across all three arms (frugality *or* correctness rules, zero tool references), and a TOOL block written from *each tool's own vendor docs* — eg from its `AGENTS.md`, cmm from its embedded docs (all three search modes, trace_path, pagination), baseline from grep/find. Parity proven mechanically by diff, both blocks independently switchable. Also upgrading `cmm-q` to actually expose semantic search and trace_path so cmm's doctrine is executable.

**2. Loop plugin, pointed at the tool not the prompt** — this is the honest path to ≥35%. The loop already proved the mechanism: snap snippets to the *true* enclosing-function boundary using the graph's own symbol spans, so one search returns the whole function instead of a fixed window (`encl_cov` 0/14 → 3/14). Since 95.9% of session tokens are context re-read, killing follow-up reads is the biggest lever the tool actually owns. An agent is now landing it properly — tests for every path, the byte-budget regression the loop's critic caught fixed, target `encl_cov` ≥ 7/14 with no ranking regression. Explicitly barred from special-casing the probe's 14 instances.

**3. Matrix sets** — nested and deterministic, committed: fable-5 ⊂ opus-10 ⊂ sonnet-20 ⊂ haiku-30, all from the official 300. Nesting means cross-model differences are model effects, not sampling luck.

Then: 4 models × 3 arms, scored on resolved% **and** tokens-per-resolved-instance, against the bar you set — accuracy > baseline, tokens < cmm, tokens ≥35% under baseline. If the frugal-prompt tool arms can't clear 35% even with the improved binary, I'll tell you that plainly rather than reshape the comparison until it passes.

Caveman plugin disabled (its `UserPromptSubmit` hook is what kept re-injecting the style). It may take a session restart to fully stop; I'm writing normally from here.

## How we got 50% before

The 54.9% came from this comparison on the official 300 (Haiku):

- **baseline arm**: stock prompt. No tool, and *no frugality instruction at all*.
- **eg arm**: search-first note, which bundles two separate things — "use this search tool to locate" **and** "reach the edit in as few turns as possible, never read a whole file, minimal fix, STOP."

So 54.9% = tool **+** frugality doctrine, measured against an agent that got neither. As a product claim ("install this, instruct your agent this way, spend half the tokens") it's defensible and it's what the number was always sold as. What it does *not* do is isolate the tool's own contribution — and that's the distinction I collided with.

Then I made it worse in the other direction: my "thorough" prompt stripped frugality from *everyone* and added "fix it properly" to everyone. Result — every arm burns turns, tools add calls on top, tools look worse than baseline. That row measures a prompt, not a tool. Neither row is the answer; the frugal row is the missing cell, and it's what's being rebuilt now.

## On cmm — you're right, and the fair record backs you

Under **identical wording** on the official 300, cmm scored **27.4% savings vs baseline** — it genuinely saves. eg scored 54.9% on the same comparison, i.e. we beat it roughly 2×. In the Sonnet thorough row eg beat cmm again (tokens 1471k vs 1554k, accuracy 22 vs 21). So "cmm saves tokens" is true against a no-frugality baseline — exactly as we do — and we're ahead of it in both fair comparisons so far.

cmm looking *worse than baseline* in that last row has two causes, both now fixed: no frugality for anyone, and our `cmm-q` wrapper exposed only BM25 search + hand-rolled Cypher while cmm actually ships `semantic_query` vector search, `trace_path`, and pagination. We were benchmarking a crippled cmm. That's being corrected before any headline number.

## Am I dogfooding? Mostly no — and the badge says so

This session: **5 search + 1 impact vs ~1,300 exploration calls, graph-first ✗, 1% of locates.** That's bad. Honest reasons: much of this work is benchmark orchestration (process management, JSON aggregation, docker) where a code graph has nothing to offer, but plenty of the code reading I *did* do went through grep/read out of habit. Brain: not used this session at all.

The subagents are worse — I only put graph doctrine into a few of the prompts. Which is precisely the gap `entire graph init-agents` exists to close, and it's why the stats command reporting "0 graph calls, high exploration" on our own repos is a finding about us, not a bug in the tool.

content.text:
That's the shipped `entire graph agent-guide` — same text `entire graph init-agents` installs into a repo's `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md`. So yes: a proper eg arm gives the agent this context, and the benchmark's eg arm was running a condensed version of it.

But look closely at those 7 rules — they're two different kinds of instruction mixed together:

**Tool-specific** (only eg can follow):
1. search first, never grep to locate
2. one search, then act
3. after search, read a line range and edit
5. `impact --symbol X` for blast radius

**Tool-agnostic** (any agent, no tool needed):
4. never read a whole file, ~120 lines max
6. don't run builds/test suites
7. every turn re-reads your context — minimize turns, stop when justified

That split is the whole fairness question. Rules 4/6/7 are pure token discipline — a grep-only baseline can follow every one of them, and when it does, most of the "savings" evaporate. Historically only the tool arms ever got them, which is how 54.9% got built.

So the design now in flight:
- **SHARED block** (4/6/7-equivalent) → byte-identical to baseline, cmm, and eg.
- **eg TOOL block** → rules 1/2/3/5, written from this guide, teaching proper `search --profile full` + `impact` usage.
- **cmm TOOL block** → its vendor equivalent, from its own docs: three combinable search modes (`query` BM25, `name_pattern` regex, `semantic_query` vector), `trace_path` for tracing, pagination via `has_more`.
- **baseline TOOL block** → grep/find locate guidance at comparable depth.

That way eg is used *properly*, cmm is used *properly*, and any remaining gap is the tool rather than the coaching. If eg still wins under that setup, the number is real and defensible — which is the only kind worth reporting.

Caveman is now fully removed — plugin entry, marketplace entry, and the cached plugin directory moved aside (`~/.claude/plugins/caveman.disabled.bak`, restorable). The style reminder you keep seeing is injected by that plugin's `UserPromptSubmit` hook into the *running* session, so it may persist until this session ends, but it can't come back after that. My own output is normal prose from here regardless.

Now — thinking hard about actually hitting the goal, because the data says the current path won't get there.

## What the numbers are telling me

Sonnet, 27 discriminating-set instances: baseline 22, eg 22, cmm 21. **19 of 27 identical across all arms; 2 unsolvable by anyone.** Only 6 instances can move at all. On that set, "beat baseline on accuracy" is barely measurable — a 1-instance swing is 3.7pt of pure noise.

Token side, thorough row: eg −19%, cmm −26% (both *worse* than baseline). Frugal row: not yet run with proper per-tool doctrine.

## Where 35% actually has to come from

Turns are the cost — 95.9% of billed tokens are context re-read, ~47.5k re-read per turn to deliver ~390 new tokens. Baseline burns **12.9 shell-explore calls/session**; eg with search-first burns **4.4**. That delta is ~8 turns × ~47k ≈ 375k tokens ≈ 30% of a 1.2M session, and it's the entire mechanism behind the original 50%. It's real, but it only materializes when the baseline is *not* also told to be frugal.

So the honest question is which baseline we're measuring against, and the answer decides whether 35% is reachable:

- vs **stock baseline** (no frugality coaching — what a real user has before installing anything): 35% is reachable; that's the 54.9% comparison, minus whatever the tool alone doesn't carry.
- vs **frugal baseline** (told "few turns, no whole-file reads, minimal fix"): the tool must beat grep on locate *efficiency alone*. The measured margin there is much thinner — 4.4 vs 12.9 explore calls is still a big edge, but the frugal baseline won't make 12.9 calls either.

Both are legitimate; they answer different questions. The frugal-baseline number is the strict one, and it's the one I'll report as the headline, with the stock-baseline number alongside as the product claim.

## The lever that makes it winnable

Zero-turn locate. If the tool supplies the ranked fix-site context *before turn 1* — the way `brain_brief` does in production — the locate phase costs zero turns instead of one search plus a read. Combined with enclosing-function snapping (kills the follow-up read) and sibling surfacing (kills the second search), that's the locate phase collapsing from ~4 turns to ~0-1 against a frugal baseline's ~4-6. That's where 35% lives, and it's a genuine tool capability, not prompt coaching.

Both agents are still landing the prerequisites (proper per-tool doctrine + `encl_cov` snapping). Next I wire the zero-turn packet as an eg arm capability, then run the matrix — haiku-30 for the accuracy signal where headroom exists, sonnet/opus/fable for tokens.

content.text:
Two findings that change the picture:

**1. A silent bug was zeroing our own arm.** `eg-q` had `prof=(); … "${prof[@]}"` — under macOS bash 3.2 with `set -u`, an empty array expansion throws `prof[@]: unbound variable`. The harness exports `EG_PROFILE=""`, so **any eg run that didn't explicitly set a profile returned an empty search, silently**, and the agent fell back to grep. My val30/s30/f30 runs all passed `EG_PROFILE=full` explicitly so they're clean, but it means the tool was one unset env var away from measuring nothing. Now defaults to `full` (what AGENTS.md prescribes).

**2. cmm was crippled two ways, both fixed.** The harness indexed with `--mode fast`, which cmm's own docs say has **no similarity/semantic edges** — one of its three search modes was silently deleted. Now `moderate`. And the wrapper exposed BM25 + hand-rolled Cypher only; it now has semantic vector search, `name_pattern` regex, `trace_path`-based callers/impact, and honest pagination.

Notably the agent also **falsified two of cmm's own marketing claims** with evidence: the three search modes do *not* combine in one call (setting `query` returns `"search_mode":"bm25"` and drops semantic results), and "bridges vocabulary — finds 'publish' when you search 'send'" doesn't reproduce (out-of-vocabulary words score ~0.00–0.10; it's lexical-embedding recall, not vocabulary bridging). Reported plainly rather than quietly benefiting from it.

**Parity is now proven by hash**, not assertion: the SHARED block is `md5 33c3cdf4…` across all three arms in frugal, `08c7818f…` across all three in thorough; each arm's TOOL block is byte-identical across families. Independent axes, exactly as designed.

One structural asymmetry worth knowing before results land: **cmm's search returns 615 B, ours 3480 B** — because ours ships source snippets and cmm ships locators only (source costs it a second `get_code_snippet` call). So cmm wins bytes-per-call while we should win turns. Since turns cost ~47k tokens each and bytes cost ~1, that trade favors us — but it has to show up in the measurement, not in my argument.

Ranking fix and encl_cov are still landing; matrix runs when they do.

Clean A/B that nails the defect — same repo, same tool, **one phrase difference**:

| query | rank 1 | rank 2 | rank 3 | rank 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| "…normalization in markdown" | **gold** `markdownUtils.ts` (12.28) | blogUtils.ts | PendingNavigation.tsx | normalization.ts |
| "…normalization in markdown**/MDX processing**" | i18n-tutorial.mdx **(22.85)** | i18n-tutorial.mdx v3.0.1 (22.85) | i18n-tutorial.mdx v3.1.1 | **gold** (demoted to #4) |

Adding "MDX" makes the token match `.mdx` *documentation* via `exact-code-token`, scoring 22.85 — nearly 2× the gold's 12.28 — and **three versioned copies of the identical tutorial** take the entire podium. The agent, following our own doctrine ("the top hit is the fix site"), goes to a translation tutorial, then searches 9 more times.

Two concrete bugs, both general and both already scoped to the ranking agent:
1. `exact-code-token` over-weights matches in prose/doc content — a filename-extension token shouldn't outrank a symbol-name + signature + path match in source.
2. No near-duplicate collapse — 3 identical versioned copies consumed 3 of 4 top slots.

This is why the frugality-vs-correctness prompt tuning kept going in circles: I was tuning agent behaviour around a ranking defect. Fixing rank-1 precision recovers *both* the lost instance and the 3.4 wasted searches/session.

## 6. Sanity check on 11.2%

**Reproduced exactly: +11.2%** (mean-of-means, n=29 common; pooled totals also 11.2%: 42,684,843 → 37,907,486). But it does not survive contact:

- **Paired per-instance: mean −0.1%, median +1.4%.** 15 wins, 14 losses.
- **Bootstrap 95% CI: −4.2% to +28.5%.** Not distinguishable from zero.
- **Top-3 instances supply 96% of the net delta.** Top-5 supply 127% (the rest is net negative).
- The single biggest contributor, `php-cs-fixer-8367` (2,601k → 91k, "saving" 2.51M = **52.5% of the whole pooled delta**), is a **degenerate 4-turn abort producing a 0-byte patch**. It saved tokens by not doing the task.
- Drop that one session: **+5.7%**. Drop the top-3 delta instances: **+0.5%**.
- Median saving is +22.5% and 10%-trimmed mean +14.1% — so eg genuinely helps the typical instance, but the mean is outlier-driven in both directions.

Honest read: **eg's real central-tendency saving is ~14–22% on median/trimmed, ~0% paired-mean, and the headline 11.2% is a coin-flip artifact.** The path to a defensible 35% is the ranked list above, not further tuning of the locate step.</result>

You're right that something's wrong, and I think I can now name it precisely — I moved the goalposts on myself.

## What actually happened to the 50%

The 54.9% (and cmm's 27.4%) were measured against a baseline that got **the stock task prompt and nothing else**. The tool arms got their tool *plus its usage doctrine* — "search first, don't grep, few turns, don't read whole files."

Then, chasing fairness, I gave the baseline **our own frugality doctrine** — the very discipline we derived from studying transcripts. That's not a neutral baseline, it's an *enhanced* one: I handed the control group our discovery and then measured how much was left. Of course it collapsed to ~5-11%. And cmm collapsed the same way (27.4% → ~4-8%) — which is exactly your instinct that cmm saves tokens; it does, against a realistic baseline.

There are two legitimate questions and I conflated them:

- **Q1 (product):** "I install this tool and follow its guide — what do I save versus my setup today?" → the 50%-class number. The doctrine is *part of the product*; a tool that teaches your agent to stop grepping is delivering real value.
- **Q2 (strict):** "Holding prompt discipline constant, what does the tool contribute?" → ~5-11%, noisy.

Both are honest. Q1 is the claim that was always being made, and it's the one your 35% target refers to. My error was reporting Q2 numbers as though the product had regressed — it hadn't; I'd changed the control.

The genuine fairness bug I *did* fix is separate and still stands: task-strategy hints ("fix properly, handle these edge cases, change every site") must not go to one arm only. That's task guidance, not tool usage. Vendor usage doctrine legitimately differs per arm — that's what the tool *is*.

content.text:
Fair question, and the honest answer is that **the original setup wasn't unfair — I mislabeled it.**

Here's the operational test I should have applied from the start. Split every instruction into two kinds:

**Tool-usage guidance** — "search first with this command", "trust the ranked result, don't re-grep to confirm", "use `impact` for blast radius". This *is* the tool. A tool you don't know how to use has no value, so its guide ships with it. Giving this only to the tool arm is not an advantage, it's the product. The baseline can't follow "search first" because it has no search.

**Task-strategy guidance** — "handle empty/nil/unicode edge cases", "change every site that needs it", "re-read your edit and check it against the issue". This is about *solving the bug*, and it has nothing to do with any tool. Give it to one arm only and you're measuring your prompt, not your tool. **That** was the real unfairness, and it was mine: my v3 "FIX IT PROPERLY" block went to the eg arm while the baseline got "implement a correct, minimal fix." When v3 beat baseline 22-18, I couldn't tell you whether the graph did that or the paragraph did.

The frugality rules sit awkwardly between the two, and that's where I got confused. "Reach the edit in few turns, don't read whole files" is genuinely part of the graph's doctrine — it's *why* the tool pays off. But it's also advice any grep-only agent can follow. So:

- Bundle it with the tool → you measure **"install this product and follow its guide"** → ~50%. Legitimate, and it's what the published number always was.
- Give it to everyone → you measure **"holding discipline constant, what does the index itself add?"** → ~5-11%, noisy. Also legitimate, and much stricter.

Neither is cheating. But I silently switched from the first to the second, then reported the drop as if the tool had regressed. That's the actual error — not the experiment design, the labeling.

The things that were genuinely unfair, and are now fixed:
- task-strategy hints to one arm only (my v3 prompt)
- cmm indexed with `--mode fast`, which its own docs say **omits semantic edges** — I was benchmarking a deliberately weakened competitor
- cmm's wrapper exposing BM25 only, no `semantic_query`, no `trace_path`
- our own `eg-q` silently returning **nothing** when `EG_PROFILE` was unset
- git history reachable in checkouts (both arms, symmetric — 3.3% vs 3.1%, so it didn't change the verdict)

So the plan now is to report both numbers side by side and say which question each answers, rather than picking the flattering one. The product comparison is running on haiku-30 right now — if the graph is healthy it should land back near the 40-55% range, and if it doesn't, that's a real regression worth chasing.

Confirmed — the full-bodies change **backfired**: more expensive on 20/29 instances, tok/turn 33.8k → 35.1k, cache_creation 31.6k → 34.0k, and turns went *up*.

The reasoning error is precise and worth naming: that agent justified a bigger payload with "tool payload is 0.6% of session spend." That's the **per-call** view. Under context replay, a byte added at turn *k* is re-read on every one of the remaining turns — its true cost is `bytes × (N−k)`, roughly **30×** at these turn counts. So a full body only pays if it removes a turn per ~1.4k tokens added. It didn't.

That inverts the design rule: payload should be **lean**, and only the top hit is worth a full body. Testing it:

input.content:
# Pre-registration — entire-graph vs codebase-memory-mcp vs no-tool baseline

Written and committed BEFORE the run it governs. An adversarial audit of the previous round found
that the reported result was the best of 21 eg configurations measured on the same 30 instances,
against 7 baseline configurations — a garden-of-forking-paths artifact (mean eg 16.2 resolved vs
mean baseline 18.3, while the published cell was eg 20 vs baseline 18). This document fixes every
degree of freedom in advance so that cannot recur.

## 1. Hypotheses

- **H1 (accuracy).** The eg arm resolves at least as many instances as the no-tool baseline.
- **H2 (tokens).** The eg arm spends fewer tokens per resolved instance than both the baseline and
  the cmm arm.
- **H3 (margin).** The eg arm spends at least 35% fewer tokens per resolved instance than baseline.

H1 and H2 are the claims. H3 is the target set for this work; it is reported as met or not met, and
a miss is reported as a miss.

## 2. Arms — exactly one configuration each, no variants

| arm | tool | prompt |
|---|---|---|
| `baseline` | none (shell + native file tools) | SHARED block + baseline TOOL block |
| `eg` | entire-graph, binary built from `main` at the sha recorded in `RUN-MANIFEST` | SHARED block + eg TOOL block |
| `cmm` | codebase-memory-mcp, indexed at its documented default `full` | SHARED block + cmm TOOL block |

- The **SHARED block is byte-identical across all three arms** (verified by md5 in the run log; it is
  emitted from a single quoted heredoc that cannot interpolate anything arm-dependent).
- Each **TOOL block** is written from that tool's own published documentation and contains only
  tool-usage guidance: which verbs exist, what they return, when to reach for which. It contains no
  task-strategy guidance (nothing about how to fix a bug, what edge cases to check, how many sites
  to change) and no turn/frugality policy — all of that lives in the SHARED block where every arm
  gets it verbatim.
- `PROMPT_FAMILY=thorough`. Chosen because the frugality clamp is a confound: it buys tokens by
  doing less work, and the previous round showed it costs resolves. Fixed in advance, not selected
  after seeing results.
- No arm is re-run for any reason other than a harness or infrastructure failure, and any re-run is
  logged with its cause in `RUN-MANIFEST`. The previous round re-ran 11 eg instances and no others;
  that will not happen again.

## 3. Instances

- **Held-out set**: 100 instances drawn from the official SWE-bench Multilingual 300, **excluding
  every instance in `.elig_val30.txt`/`.elig_h30.txt`** — the set the prompt variants v3…v9 were
  iterated against. Selection is deterministic: sort the eligible instance ids lexicographically and
  take the first 100 that have a prebuilt entire-graph dump AND a resolvable docker eval image.
- The list is frozen to `.elig_prereg100.txt` and committed **before** the run starts.
- Instances where entire-graph fails to build a graph are **scored as an eg loss**, not excluded.
  A tool that cannot index the repo has failed at its job; the previous round silently excluded
  10/300 such instances.
- Instances whose docker eval image is unavailable upstream (e.g. `nushell__nushell-13831`) are
  excluded from **all** arms and named in the report.

## 4. Replication

**3 independent runs per arm** (`_r1`, `_r2`, `_r3`). All statistics are computed on the per-arm
**mean across runs**; single-run numbers are reported only as spread. The previous round's headline
rested on single runs whose per-instance bootstrap CI spanned zero in both directions.

## 5. Gate — applied identically to every arm

An instance counts for an arm when that arm's session has `total_cost_usd > 0` **and** a non-empty
`patch.diff`. A gate failure is scored as **unresolved for that arm** and the instance stays in the
denominator for every arm. The previous round intersected arms after gating, which let one arm's
empty patch delete an instance the competitor had resolved — that inverted the eg-vs-cmm result.

## 6. Metrics

- **Primary:** resolved count on the common graded set, per arm, mean of 3 runs.
- **Secondary:** total tokens per instance (`input + cache_creation + cache_read + output`),
  tokens per resolved instance, USD per resolved instance.
- **Turns** reported as the mechanism, not a claim.

## 7. Analysis — fixed in advance

- Paired per-instance comparison; **bootstrap 95% CI (20,000 resamples over instances)** for every
  token claim.
- **McNemar exact test** for every resolved-count claim.
- A claim is reported as **supported** only if its CI excludes zero (tokens) or p < 0.05 (resolves).
  Anything else is reported as "not distinguishable from zero" with the interval shown.
- Every headline is also reported with its **leave-one-instance-out range**, since the previous
  round's eg-vs-cmm token result flipped sign on the removal of a single instance.

## 8. What gets published

The pre-registered configuration's numbers, whatever they are. If eg loses, the report says eg
loses. Exploratory configurations (the frugality clamp, payload variants, prompt families) may be
reported in an appendix, explicitly labelled exploratory, and never as the headline.

## 9. Known asymmetries, disclosed

- entire-graph ships an agent guide containing turn-economics coaching; cmm's documentation does
  not. In this pre-registered design that material sits in the SHARED block, so all three arms get
  it and the comparison is of tools, not guides. A separate, clearly-labelled control arm
  (`CMM_DISCIPLINE`) exists to quantify the guide's contribution and is appendix material.
- eg's search returns source inline; cmm's returns locators. The wrappers were brought to parity of
  usable information before this run; the before/after byte accounting is in the run log.

Decisive result, and it **falsifies my hypothesis**. Six arms, n=27:

| arm | resolved | tok/instance | tok/resolved | turns |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| baseline | 18/27 (66.7%) | 1,390k | 2,085k | 33.9 |

**My hypothesis was wrong.** I predicted the clamp's accuracy cost was a symptom of bad ranking. With ranking repaired, the clamp costs **more**: −11.1pp (55.6% vs 66.7%) versus −6.3pp on the old tool. The mechanism isn't ranking, it's **early stopping** — clamp median 12 turns, and 9/27 sessions quit at ≤6 turns. It abandons anything needing real investigation: `axum-691` quit at 4 turns/87k where the baseline spent 35 turns and solved it.

**And the control answers your cmm question definitively.** Our discipline text moves cmm almost not at all (−3.4% tokens, 19→18 resolves). Unguided, **the two indexes are within 1.0% on tokens and 1 resolve of each other** (eg 1,226k/20R vs cmm 1,238k/19R). The large swings are all *guide*, not index — and the guide only pays on our tool because the model will actually trust one eg search and stop. That trust is exactly what costs the 5 resolves.

## Goal status: not met, and the target now looks structurally hard

The two requirements pull against each other through one variable:

- accuracy-winning arm (verbs-only): **20/27**, tokens −11.8%/instance, −20.6%/resolved
- token-winning arm (clamp): **−61.8%/instance, −54.2%/resolved**, but 15/27

No arm does both. And the ceiling analysis says closing conversion fully to baseline's rate at our current locate rate projects ~147 vs baseline's 150 on the 300 — parity, not a win.

I'll keep pushing the honest lever (related-sites is still landing; the verify doctrine now ships), but I want to flag plainly: **a single configuration that beats baseline on accuracy *and* by ≥35% tokens may not exist here.** What does exist, and is defensible, is a Pareto pair — same tool, two operating points, both documented with CIs. Tell me if you want me to keep hunting the single-config win or write up the frontier.

1. Lexical retrieval over identifiers and source text with `search` is precise and seems to excellently return vertical
   slices. Searching for something specific like "update <entity>" returns the backend function that has the domain
   logic for the update at rank 1, but ranks 2-10 also trace the whole vertical call/domain slice all the way to the UI
   components. Docstring phrasing works just as well as identifiers.

   See **D8** for the significant caveat: query *phrasing* seems to behave the opposite of how `agent-guide`
   recommends writing queries, at least in my testing.

2. `impact` is probably the most valuable command. One call returns blast radius, direct *and* transitive callers with
   `via` attribution, type consumers by relation kind, data flows, siblings, and — amazingly — **git co-change
   coupling**. Here's an example. 0.2 s on a warm cache. "Which test file will I need to touch" answered without asking.

   ```
   Impact: buildGroupIndex (<full-path>/grouped-selection.ts:17) [function]
   Blast radius: 8 callers (5 direct, 3 transitive), 0 callees, 4 type consumers, 0 data flows,
                 4 co-change files, 0 siblings.
   Co-change coupling (4; files that historically change with grouped-selection.ts):
   - <full-path>/__tests__/grouped-selection.test.ts [changed together in 5 recent commits]
   ```

3. **Line-anchored snippets with symbol names and `[focus:N]`.** Results land an agent directly on an editable range.
   Compared to tools that return node IDs or whole-file pointers, this is the difference between a usable result and a
   starting point for more searching.

4. **Freshness with no rebuild step.** Worktree mode found a brand-new, uncommitted, never-saved symbol at rank 1 in 0.8
   s. graphify needed a 20.5 s full re-extract before it could see the same file.

5. **Honest completeness reporting.** `partial_failures`, `completeness_level: degraded`, and per-file
   `effect_on_semantic_completeness` mean the agent can tell when an answer is thin instead of guessing. Same for
   `stats` printing its estimation assumption inline ("Model (assumption, not a measurement)") next to the number.

6. **Zero repo footprint.** everything in `%LOCALAPPDATA%`, nothing to commit, merge, or gitignore. graphify keeps a 4.6
   MB `graph.json` + 3.6 MB `graph.html` under version control with a pre-commit stage hook and a git merge driver.

### D1 — `export const fn = () => {}` is mis-extracted, making the symbol permanently un-queryable (**highest impact**)

`impact` and `neighbors` refuse to answer when a symbol name resolves to more than one definition. For the
`export const NAME = <arrow function>` idiom that refusal is triggered by an extractor bug, and neither remedy the error
message suggests can resolve it.

```console
$ entire graph impact --repo . --symbol markDashboardsAsStale --head --profile full
Ambiguous symbol "markDashboardsAsStale" matched 2 definitions; rerun with --file and, if needed, a qualified --symbol.
- markDashboardsAsStale (<full-path>/DashboardStore.tsx:82)
- markDashboardsAsStale (<full-path>/DashboardStore.tsx:83)
```

The two "definitions" are one real symbol, and the underlying records show two separate problems. From
`entire graph symbols --format ndjson`:

```json
{
  "kind": "variable",
  "name": "markDashboardsAsStale",
  "qualified_name": "markDashboardsAsStale",
  "file_path": "...DashboardStore.tsx",
  "start_line": 82,
  "end_line": 82,
  "signature": ""
}
{
  "kind": "function",
  "name": "markDashboardsAsStale",
  "qualified_name": "markDashboardsAsStale",
  "file_path": "...DashboardStore.tsx",
  "start_line": 83,
  "end_line": 96,
  "signature": "markDashboardsAsStale = (pendingParameters: Parameter[] = []) =>"
}
```

Against the source:

```ts
81: }
82:                                        // <- the "variable" record points here
83: export const markDashboardsAsStale = (pendingParameters: Parameter[] = []) => {
```

**Bug 1 — off-by-one on the `variable` record.** For `export const NAME = <arrow function>`, the
`variable` record is emitted at `declaration_line − 1` with `start_line == end_line` and an empty
`signature`. This is deterministic, not an edge case. Across our repo:

| Measurement                                                                              | Count  |
|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------|
| `variable`+`function` pairs for this idiom                                               | 31     |
| …where the `variable` record lands on a **blank line** at exactly `declaration_line − 1` | **29** |
| …where both records instead stack on the same one-line declaration                       | **29** |

The remaining 2 are single-line arrow functions (e.g. `export const getToken = () => getAuthToken()`), where variable
and function records share the declaration line. For the 29 there is no reading in which a symbol occupies only a blank
line, so the line attribution is simply wrong.

**Bug 2 — the pair should never have been ambiguous.** A `const` binding and the function expression initialising it are
*one entity*. Worse, both records share `name` **and** `qualified_name`, so the two remedies the error message names are
structurally incapable of resolving it:

- `--file` cannot help — both records are in the same file.
- a qualified `--symbol` cannot help — the qualified names are byte-identical.

I tried `function:markDashboardsAsStale`, `markDashboardsAsStale()`, and
`DashboardStore.markDashboardsAsStale`; all returned `No symbols matched "…". Add --file to disambiguate a
known definition.` — which routes you straight back to the failure you started from.

**Scope.** 148 of 4,082 symbols (3.6%) have >1 record for the same `(file, name)` and therefore cannot be queried by
`impact`/`neighbors` at all. 31 of those are this idiom — and `export const fn = () => {}` is the dominant
function-declaration style in a modern TypeScript codebase, so the practical hit rate on the symbols an agent actually
wants is far higher than 3.6% suggests.

**Suggestion:** correct the `variable` record's line attribution and collapse a variable-binding + its
function-expression initialiser into a single symbol.

### D2 — Worktree mode ignores `.gitignore`

`--head` respects `.gitignore` correctly (676 files). The **default** worktree mode does not, and pulls in vendored
dependencies and — notably — Entire's own session transcripts.

```console
$ entire graph search --repo . --profile full --query "grouped destination multi-select combobox" --format agent
Coverage: degraded (8 languages/74 files; 1 warning; 6 partial failures)
- partial E_PARSE_ERROR: backend/.venv/Lib/site-packages/numpy/_core/include/numpy/__multiarray_api.h
```

And on another query, ranks 3 and 5 were:

```
3. .entire/metadata/5c6819a1-.../full.jsonl:230 [focus:230]
5. .entire/metadata/5c6819a1-.../full.jsonl:503 [focus:503]
```

`.entire/metadata/` is listed in `.entire/.gitignore`. The graph indexing its own metadata and returning it as a
code-search hit displaces real results in the top 10.

To size the problem, I had the agent dump the worktree snapshot (`entire graph snapshot --repo . --format ndjson
--worktree`): it had crawled **20,326 files and written 671 MB of NDJSON** before we killed it — 5,050 files under
`.venv` trees alone, `.pytest_cache` directories, and `.entire/tmp`, every sampled path confirmed ignored via
`git check-ignore -v`. This walk is very plausibly the bulk of D3's worktree cost too — a walker that respects
`.gitignore` would likely fix most of both defects at once.

### D3 — Worktree mode cache-misses on every invocation (~52 s per query)

```
--head      : Index: cache-hit  (207ms)  | Query: 11692ms | Preselect:   303ms | Total: 12203ms
default     : Index: cache-miss (18730ms)| Query: 13100ms | Preselect: 19866ms | Total: 51697ms
default (2nd, identical query, no file changes)
            : Index: cache-miss (21570ms)| Query: 15521ms | Preselect: 14847ms | Total: 51938ms
```

Two identical back-to-back runs with an unchanged worktree both missed. If the cache key includes a worktree hash, it
seems not to be stable across runs; if worktree results are simply never cached, a dirty tree makes every search a ~52 s
operation.

This matters more than the raw number because **`entire graph agent-guide` recommends exactly this command** — without
`--head`. The doctrine's headline command is the slow, `.gitignore`-ignoring path.

**Suggestion:** Either make worktree mode cacheable, or have `agent-guide` recommend `--head` with worktree as the
explicit opt-in for uncommitted code.

### D4 — `--format agent` hides the relevance score, which is the only no-match signal

Search always returns results with no "nothing matched" state. I ran a nonsense control — a query about technology that
does not exist anywhere in my repo — and got six confident, well-formatted hits, indistinguishable in presentation from
a real answer:

```console
$ entire graph search ... --query "kubernetes ingress controller rate limiting middleware" --format agent
1. <a TypeScript SSE configuration>
2. <our website's privacy page component>
3. <a completely unrelated Python business logic function>
```

The good news: `--format json` already exposes a `score` that an agent could use to discriminate the results:

| Query                         | Top-3 scores          |
|-------------------------------|-----------------------|
| Real target present in repo   | `35.34  33.27  33.15` |
| Diffuse architecture question | `13.96  13.39  12.71` |
| Nonsense control              | `9.60  8.38  8.10`    |

**Caveat, and arguably a second bug:** these numbers hold only at the default `--top-k`. Pass `--top-k 11`
or higher and `score` is silently replaced by `1/rank` — `1, 0.5, 0.333, …` — identical for a perfect query and the
nonsense control:

```console
$ ... --top-k 10 --format json   # real scores
35.337  33.271  33.145
$ ... --top-k 11 --format json   # same query, same index
1  0.5  0.333
```

And it is not just a display bug — the run's own stats block shows `--top-k ≥ 11` switches to a different retrieval path
entirely: `preselection_backend` flips from `git-tree-grep` to `go-content`,
`files_content_read_during_preselection` goes from 0 to 736 (every file in the repo), `files_indexed`
drops 326 → 96, and preselect latency grows ~8×. Deduplication also stops: at `--top-k 11` the same symbol
(`service.py:195 update_market_sizes`) occupies ranks 1, 2 **and** 3, and the 11 rows contain only 9 unique locations.
So above 10 you get placeholder scores, duplicate rows, and a slower, thinner index — and since the usage text documents
`[--top-k 20]` while the actual default is 10, the documented value sits inside the broken regime.

So the signal exists — it's just withheld from the format aimed at agents. Combined with `agent-guide`'s instruction (
"The top hit is the fix site on most tasks — go straight there and edit; do NOT re-search or grep to confirm"), an agent
asked about something absent from the repo might be tempted to edit the SSE configuration on a completely unrelated ask.

Nothing else in the output substitutes for the score: the `Coverage: degraded` header is *parse* coverage and appears
identically on good queries, and the JSON `warnings` array is `[]` in both cases.

**Suggestion:** surface `score` in `--format agent`, emit an explicit low-confidence banner below a threshold (or
document a recommended cutoff in `agent-guide`), and keep real scores — and deduplication — alive above `--top-k 10`.

### D5 — Markdown files become phantom callers, and phantom edges compound transitively

Markdown files are reported as callers. `impact` on `buildGroupIndex` (used in code only in Combobox.tsx):

```
Callers (5 direct, 3 transitive; who breaks if behavior changes):
- 2026-07-24-grouped-destination-multi-select.md (docs/superpowers/plans/...)
- Combobox (<full-path>/Combobox.tsx:138)
- grouped-selection.test.ts (<full-path>/__tests__/grouped-selection.test.ts)
...
- DESIGN.md (intents/grouped-destination-multi-select/DESIGN.md) [via Combobox]
...
```

The *direct* Markdown callers are defensible in a way — the superpowers plan doc contains genuine call syntax of
`buildGroupIndex` inside fenced code blocks. But the *transitive* callers should, in my opinion, not be listed by
`impact`: `DESIGN.md` contains zero occurrences of the string `buildGroupIndex`. It is pulled in because a `name_only`
file-level edge onto `Combobox` is traversed a second hop — documents that never name the function are reported as
things that "break if behavior changes". A doc file cannot break either way.

The provenance to fix this already exists: `neighbors` labels these edges `[file-level, name_only]` in text output and
carries `"resolution": "name_only", "confidence": 0.68` in JSON (note: `neighbors` defaults to JSON; the labels shown
above need `--format text`). `impact` alone discards the distinction — a presentation bug, not a missing-data bug. On a
well-documented symbol these entries crowd out real callers within `--limit`.

**Suggestion:** exclude `name_only` matches from prose/inventory-only languages in `impact` — certainly from transitive
expansion — or rank them last and label them.

### D6 — `diff`/`analyze` cannot see uncommitted work

```console
$ git diff --stat
 <changed-file-path> | 2 +-

$ entire graph analyze --repo . --base HEAD
Semantic changes HEAD..HEAD
No semantic entity changes detected.
```

`--base HEAD` silently degrades to `HEAD..HEAD` rather than comparing HEAD against the worktree —
`entire graph diff --base HEAD --json` returns `{"base": "HEAD", "head": "HEAD", "files": null}`. The pending edits were
not semantically trivial: one removes a whole top-level JSON key, exactly the "section removed" shape `analyze`
demonstrably reports across committed ranges.

Guessing at the fix makes it worse: `analyze --base HEAD --worktree` exits 0 with the same "No semantic entity changes
detected." — `analyze`/`diff` silently swallow **any** unrecognized flag (`--zzznotaflag` behaves identically), while
`search` correctly rejects unknown arguments with exit 1. A silent no-op that reads as a confident "no changes" answer
is more dangerous than an error. The flag surface is inconsistent underneath: `--head` is a boolean on `search`/
`impact`/`neighbors` but takes a rev value on `diff`/`analyze`, and no spelling on any of them names the worktree. Since
`snapshot`, `symbols`, and `edges` all accept `--worktree`, its omission on `diff`/`analyze` looks unintentional. This
is the gap that matters most for pre-commit review: the natural question is "what did I semantically change *before* I
commit," which is unanswerable at this point.

### D7 — No persistent ignore configuration

`--ignore-file` must be passed on every invocation, and passing it **changes the cache key**, forcing one re-index per
distinct ignore config (`cache-miss (8136ms)`; identical reruns then cache-hit, so the cost is one-time rather than
per-call — but forget the flag once and you silently query a differently-scoped index). It is also undocumented on
`search` (usage lists it only on
`snapshot`/`symbols`/`edges`/`index`) yet accepted there. A `graph.ignore` block in
`.entire/settings.json` — folded into the cache key once — would resolve this and D2 together.

**Found while verifying this:** passing *any* `--ignore-file` breaks the Coverage header. With a one-line ignore file
the header reports `Coverage: degraded (3 languages/96 files …)` — and an ignore file matching nothing at all still
reports 96 files — while the results prove the index still covers the full repo. Whatever census feeds the header is
computed over something else entirely once the flag is passed.

### D8 — Unmatched query terms are *penalised* rather than ignored, and there is no stemming

This is a long one, sorry about that. It started as an observation that natural-language queries perform badly and that
`agent-guide`'s `"<the task or bug in one sentence>"` guidance was therefore wrong. On investigation that framing was
backwards: the guidance is reasonable, but the scorer is the problem. Three separable issues.

**D8a — adding a term that matches nothing lowers the score of a document that already matched.**
This is the root cause, and it is easy to reproduce. All runs `--head --profile full --top-k 10`.

| Query                            | Target rank            | Target score |
|----------------------------------|------------------------|--------------|
| `update market sizes`            | **1**                  | **40.10**    |
| `update market sizes please`     | **absent from top 10** | —            |
| `update market sizes xyzzy`      | **absent from top 10** | —            |
| `update the market sizes`        | 4                      | 26.10        |
| `update market sizes please now` | **absent from top 10** | —            |

One stopword removes a rank-1 hit. A nonsense token (`xyzzy`) that appears nowhere in the repo does the same. The effect
is proportional and visible on a stronger match too:

| Query                    | Target rank | Target score     |
|--------------------------|-------------|------------------|
| `buildGroupIndex`        | 1           | 79.25            |
| `buildGroupIndex please` | 1           | **61.56** (−22%) |

So a term absent from the corpus contributes a *negative* signal. In BM25 and friends such a term contributes ~0 — it
cannot hurt a document that matched the other terms. The JSON `signals` array shows the actual mechanism: the rank-1 hit
for `buildGroupIndex` carries `[body, exact-symbol, symbol-name, exact-code-token, all-query-terms]`; add `please` and
the same hit shrinks to `[body, symbol-name, exact-code-token]` — the unmatched token revokes both the `exact-symbol`
and `all-query-terms` bonuses the document had already earned. And the penalty is generic, not linguistic: `… please`
and `… xyzzy` return byte-identical result sets in identical order. On a strong match (~80) the target survives the
penalty; on a moderate one (~40) it drops out of the results entirely.

**This single bug explains the entire "natural language doesn't work" symptom.** A question like
`"how do I update the market sizes"` contains four tokens (`how`, `do`, `I`, `the`) that match nothing, and each one
taxes the score — even though the content words are identical to the query that scores 40.1 and ranks 1.

**Suggestion:** Make unmatched tokens contribute zero — instead of revoking earned bonuses — and `agent-guide`'s
one-sentence guidance should work as designed.

**D8b — no stemming or lemmatisation.** Case folding and identifier splitting *are* implemented, so the normalisation
pipeline exists; it is just missing the morphology stage:

| Query                      | Target rank | Note                                                                                                                               |
|----------------------------|-------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `UPDATE MARKET SIZES`      | 2–3         | case folding works for matching — but see below                                                                                    |
| `updateMarketSizes`        | 6–10        | camelCase splitting works; the frontend wrapper `updateMarketSizes` takes rank 1 and the backend target barely stays in the window |
| `update-market-sizes`      | 3           | kebab splitting works                                                                                                              |
| `update_market_sizes`      | 2           | exact identifier, score 75.24                                                                                                      |
| **`updating market size`** | **absent**  | gerund + singular breaks it                                                                                                        |

Case folding also turns out not to be score-neutral: `UPDATE MARKET SIZES` scores the same symbol at **2.1×** the
identical lowercase query (93.9 vs 44.6 on re-verification). Matching survives the case change; the score doubles for no
reason.

**D8c — no synonym or semantic matching, and `hybrid_source_search` is misleading.** A single verb substitution, with
the noun phrase left intact, loses the target completely:

| Query                         | Target rank |
|-------------------------------|-------------|
| `update market sizes`         | 1           |
| `modify market sizes`         | absent      |
| `update market dimensions`    | absent      |
| `change the size of a market` | absent      |

`capabilities --json` advertises `"optional_local_only_features": {"hybrid_source_search": true, …}`, which I initially
read as lexical + semantic. In fact, "semantic" is the entire promise of the graph tool ("semantic checkpoint context
plugin", "Semantic diff between two refs", etc.). But "semantic search", which is what someone could reasonably assume
the tool does based on its description, is something completely different – vector-based matching of context and intent.
And by extension "hybrid search", which the plugin does actually use explicitly ("Find the code for this task → search
(hybrid, ranked)"), is the "official" industry term for lexical + semantic (i.e. vector-based) search. But the on-disk
cache contains only gzipped JSON (`search/search-snapshot-v4/*.json.gz` plus `records/provider-records-v1/`; 36 files,
~5.8 MB at last measure) — a scan for `*.bin`/`*.onnx`/`*.safetensors`/`*.faiss` and friends returns nothing, and a
decompressed snapshot holds only files/symbols/relations — so based on this and the above verb-substitution test, I
assume that "hybrid" in Entire means *symbol matching + raw source-text matching* – both lexical, and NOT semantic, at
least not in the sense the term is typically used in the context of text retrieval methods.

**Suggestion:** If I'm wrong on this, please let me know – but I don't think I am because then the above search terms
SHOULD return the target at least somewhere in the top 10. **Please explain this in `capabilities`/docs**, because the
current flag name reads as a semantic-search claim that the engine does not make good on, and it changes how much an
agent should trust a paraphrased query.

**Priority note:** I would fix D8a first and independently — it is a change to when the `exact-symbol`/`all-query-terms`
bonuses apply, not a retrieval-engine redesign, and it is the difference between "agents must learn to phrase queries
like a search engine from 2004" and "agents can ask the question they actually have."

---

## Smaller notes

- **`E_FILE_TOO_LARGE` at 4 MB.** A 4.66 MB JSON in our repo (the previous graphify data) is skipped entirely.
  Reasonable default, but a `--max-file-bytes` override would help repos with large generated fixtures.
- **Windows/Git Bash worked without issue.** Applause for this, graphify was not as charitable. No path-separator or
  line-ending problems in any command.
- **`--profile full` cold index:** ~30 s for 676 files. Entirely acceptable (get it?). Warm `--head` calls are 0.2 s.

That feedback is gold, and one item in it is likely *the* cause of our accuracy problem.

**D8a: unmatched query terms are penalized rather than ignored.** Their measurements:

```
update market sizes          → rank 1, score 40.10
update market sizes please   → absent from top 10
update market sizes xyzzy    → absent from top 10
buildGroupIndex              → rank 1, 79.25
buildGroupIndex please       → rank 1, 61.56 (−22%)
```

A token that appears nowhere in the corpus **revokes** the `exact-symbol` and `all-query-terms` bonuses the document already earned. In BM25 an unmatched term contributes ~0; it cannot hurt.

Now connect that to our benchmark: our harness tells the agent to search `"<the bug in one sentence>"` — sentences full of `how`, `the`, `when`, `should`, plus issue-specific nouns that don't exist in the code. **Every stopword taxes the score.** That is a very plausible explanation for top-1 precision sitting at 57% and for the "wrong site picked off the ranked list" failure class (5 of 31 losses). Fixing it is a locate-quality lever we haven't touched, and it comes from an external user, not from tuning on eval instances.

On your clamp question — yes, and the data says exactly how to adapt it. The clamp's win is real (−54% tokens/resolved) and its loss is **early stopping**, not bad ranking: median 12 turns, 9/27 sessions quit at ≤6, and within the clamp arm resolved sessions averaged 11.5 turns while failures averaged 21.9. So the fix isn't "clamp less", it's **clamp exploration but forbid stopping until verified and swept**:
